verses.1:
Al-Mizan describes this chapter as a summons to true belief and good deeds, combining warning and glad tidings, and culminating in the command that one who hopes to meet his Lord should do good deeds and associate no one in His service (18:110). Its special warning against those who say that God has taken a son follows the general warning of punishment. It addresses idolaters who call angels, and perhaps jinn and human reformers (muṣliḥīn), God’s sons; Christians who call the Messiah God’s son; and perhaps Jews who attribute partners to Him, including the claim that ʿUzayr (Ezra) is God’s son (9:30).

The chapter’s three stories—the Companions of the Cave (aṣḥāb al-kahf), Moses and his servant’s journey to where the seas meet, and Dhū l-Qarnayn—occur nowhere else in the Qur’an. Their lessons are to be applied to the chapter’s refutation of partnership with God and its call to mindfulness of Him. Its context indicates a Meccan revelation, apart from the verse beginning, And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord (18:28).

On “(All) praise is due to God who revealed the Book to His servant and did not make in it any crookedness,” Al-Mizan explains that ʿiwaj denotes crookedness, especially in what is apprehended intellectually, such as religion or speech; its use in You shall not see therein any crookedness (ʿiwajan) or unevenness. (20:107) does not contradict this. God praises Himself for revealing the Qur’an to His servant free of every deviation from truth, a Book that serves people’s interests in this world and the next. The good and rectitude found in human society derive from the prophets’ call to truth, good character, and good deeds; the Qur’an and the message have refined society and encouraged useful knowledge and righteous action. Thus the verse is actual divine praise, not an implied command to the Prophet to say, “Praise is due to God.”

The pronoun in “did not make in it any crookedness” refers to the Qur’an, and the clause describes the Book. “Rightly directing” (Qayyiman) in the following verse is a second, equally emphasized description of it: the Book has no crookedness and directs human society to its best interests. Interpretations that make qayyiman a circumstantial qualification dependent on another clause, or that rearrange the verse to mean merely that God revealed the Book properly, divide the intended emphasis and contradict the context; the latter is the worst explanation. The negation of crookedness precedes the affirmation that the Book is rightly directing because freedom from defect is perfection itself, while right direction brings perfection about.

Because ʿiwajan is indefinite after negation, the Qur’an is straight in every respect: lucid in wording, eloquent in meaning, correct in guidance, vigorous in proofs, admonitory in commands and prohibitions, truthful in narratives and glad tidings, decisive in judgment, immune from corruption and discrepancy, and inaccessible to falsehood from before or behind.

Al-qayyim is one who manages another’s affairs and interests. The Qur’an is qayyim through its content of true belief and good practice (al-ʿamal al-ṣāliḥ), guiding to truth and a straight path (46:30). It is so called because Islam is the right religion and serves humanity’s worldly and otherworldly good; perhaps the Book was first called qayyim and the religion then described accordingly in . . . and that is the right religion (dīn al-qayyima) (98:5), understood metaphorically as the religion of the true books (dīn al-kutub al-qayyima). Other explanations—that qayyim means even and without neglect or excess, or that it oversees, confirms, preserves, or repeals the laws of prior heavenly books—are reported, but the concluding warning and glad tidings support the first explanation.

The Book warns of severe punishment, apparently including everyone who fails to do righteous deeds: outright unbelievers and believing sinners alike. The glad tidings are specifically for believers who do good deeds, and their “goodly reward,” in which they remain forever, is plainly heaven. Its ability to set matters right, warn, and give glad tidings explains why the Book was revealed in this perfect condition.

The particular warning to those who claim that God has taken a son highlights their doctrine after the general warning. Their claim concerns literal begetting, as shown by: How could He have a son when He has no consort, while He (Himself) created everything, and He is the One who knows all things? (6:101). God refutes it by denying that either they or their forefathers have knowledge and by declaring their speech a lie. They had appealed to their supposedly more knowledgeable ancestors and followed their footsteps; the verse separately denies knowledge to both followers and forefathers. Their utterance is grievous because it ascribes a partner to God and entails corporeality, composition, and need for a helper or vicegerent.

Al-Mizan considers it possible that such language originated in honorific references to people as God’s sons, as in claims about ʿUzayr or “We are God’s children and His beloved (5:18),” or in allegories calling the first creation a son, or the means of coming into being a wife; hence some early angels were termed wives, sons, and daughters. Even where these latter expressions were honorific allegories rather than literal begetting, the shariah forbids them, since they lead to everlasting misery and eternal doom.

“Then maybe you will kill (bākhiʿun) yourself with grief over them if they do not believe in this announcement” consoles and encourages the Prophet. Bukhūʿ and bakhʿ mean killing or consuming, āthār are tracks, asaf is severe grief, and “this announcement” is the Qur’an. The fāʾ connects the verse to their disbelief and rejection of God’s signs. It fears that the Prophet will be consumed by grief as they turn their backs on the Qur’an and on him; ʿalā āthārihim, literally “over their tracks,” metaphorically denotes that turning away.

The earth’s adornment (zīnatan lahā)—all that makes it beautiful and desirable—is a divine test to disclose who is best in deeds. Ṣaʿīd is the earth’s surface, and juruz is barren ground that appears to devour all growth. Human souls, though sublime and not naturally inclined to earthly life, attain perfection and eternal happiness through true belief and good deeds. God therefore places them on earth for a fixed term, binds their hearts to its beloved attractions—wealth, children, prestige, and other pleasures—and tests and purifies them through the choice to which these attachments give rise.

When their appointed earthly term and trial end, God removes their attachment to the earth’s finery, effaces its beauty, and leaves it barren, without vegetation or bloom; they return alone as they were first created. This is His recurring way with generations and individuals: earthly pleasures are made attractive so that the worthy are distinguished, then people are cut off from those pleasures and transferred from the abode of toil to punishment and reward. The cited descriptions of death and return alone to God express this severing of ties.

Thus these verses further console the Prophet: those absorbed in worldly pleasures and turning from his warnings and glad tidings are undergoing divine preparation and testing, not frustrating a divine will that all should believe. “We will make what is on it bare ground without herbage” is chiefly a metaphor for cutting human attachment to worldly pleasures, though it may also mean that the earth’s actual adornments will be reduced to dust and level ground. The explicit wording “what is on it,” rather than simply “it,” perhaps draws attention to the fact that the adornment is upon the earth. God willed their trial, and His will and power prevail.

The Qur’an is rightly directing (qayyim) through its content: true belief and good practice (al-ʿamal al-ṣāliḥ), which guide to truth and to a straight path (46:30). It is described thus because Islam is the right religion, serving humanity’s welfare in this world and the hereafter. Perhaps the Book was first characterized as qayyim and the religion later called so in . . . and that is the right religion (dīn al-qayyima) (98:5), understood metaphorically as the religion of the true books (dīn al-kutub al-qayyima).

Other reported explanations define al-qayyim as straight and even, free from neglect and excess, or as the Book responsible for earlier heavenly books by confirming and preserving them or repealing their legal codes. Yet the conclusion that it warns of severe punishment and gives believers glad tidings supports the first explanation.

The warning apparently extends to all who fail to perform righteous deeds: both unbelievers and believers who commit sins. This follows from the fact that the promised believers are qualified as those who do good deeds. The Book’s intrinsic rectitude and its power to put matters right, warn, and give glad tidings explain why it was revealed perfectly. The “goodly reward,” in which they remain forever, means heaven.

verses.5:
Al-Mizan holds that the claim that God has a son means literal begetting, as indicated by: How could He have a son when He has no consort, while He (Himself) created everything, and He is the One who knows all things? (6:101). God refutes it by declaring that it rests on no knowledge and that it is a lie. The denial of knowledge applies both to those making the claim and to their forefathers, whom they invoke as more knowledgeable authorities whose religion and footsteps they merely follow.

The phrase “A grievous word it is that comes out of their mouths” rebukes the claim’s enormity and its audacity toward God: it associates a partner with Him and implies that He is corporeal, compounded, and in need of a helper or vicegerent.

Al-Mizan considers it possible that the language began with honorific references to persons as God’s son, as in the claims concerning ʿUzayr and “We are God’s children and His beloved (5:18),” to signify nearness to God. It may also have arisen from allegorically calling the first creation a son because it came from God, or calling the means of coming into being a wife and, accordingly, some first-created angels wives, sons, or daughters. Although such latter expressions may be honorific allegories and less grave than literal begetting, the shariah still prohibits them because they lead people to everlasting misery and eternal doom.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that this verse, together with the following two, consoles and encourages the Prophet. Bukhūʿ and bakhʿ mean killing or consuming; āthār are tracks; asaf is severe grief; and “this announcement” means the Qur’an. The fāʾ connects the verse to the people’s disbelief and rejection of God’s signs. It expresses fear that the Prophet will be consumed by profound grief when they turn their backs on the Qur’an and on him; ʿalā āthārihim, literally “over their tracks,” is a metaphor for that turning away.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains zīna as an ornament or embellishment added to make something beautiful and desirable; ṣaʿīd as the earth’s surface; and, according to Majmaʿ al-bayān, juruz as barren earth that seems to devour all growth. The verses set out the reality of earthly human existence. Though human souls are sublime and noble and would not otherwise incline toward earth and its life, God decreed that their perfection and eternal happiness lie in true belief and good deeds. He therefore places them on earth for an appointed term as a site of action, purification, and testing, and makes them attached to beloved worldly pleasures such as wealth, children, and prestige. These attractive things are the earth’s adornment, through which souls cling to earthly life.

When the divinely appointed term and trial have ended, God removes the attachment between people and the earth’s pleasures, erases its finery, and makes the earth barren, without vegetation or bloom. They are then summoned to journey alone as they were first created. This is God’s recurring way with generations and individuals: He makes worldly pleasures attractive, leaves people to choose, and thereby distinguishes the honorable from others; then, after the test, He cuts them off from those ornaments and transfers them from the abode of toil to the abode of punishment and reward. The cited scenes of death and coming to God alone describe this severance.

The verses consequently console the Prophet not to grieve for people who turn away from his warnings and glad tidings while absorbed in worldly pleasure. Their life is a divinely arranged test, not evidence that God willed universal faith and was defeated by their rejection and prolonged misguidance. He willed that they be tried, and His will and power prevail.

“Most surely We will make what is on it bare ground without herbage” is primarily a metaphorical allusion to the cutting of people’s attachment to earthly pleasures. It may also mean literally reducing the earth’s finery to dust and leveling it into smooth, barren ground. The explicit phrase “what is on it,” rather than simply “it,” perhaps emphasizes that the adornment is upon the earth.

verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that ḥusbān means thinking; kahf is a mountain cave, larger than a ghār; and raqīm means writing or inscription. The Companions of the Cave and the Inscription are apparently one prominent group, called aṣḥāb al-kahf because they entered the cave and what occurred there, and aṣḥāb al-raqīm because their account was inscribed on a plaque displayed or preserved in the king’s archive. Other reports identify al-Raqīm as the mountain, its valley, the place to which they first fled, or their dog, but the inscribed record is preferred.

The commentary rejects the view that the Companions of the Inscription were a separate group whose story is not related here. It is extremely unlikely, given the Qur’an’s eloquence, that both groups would be named while only one was discussed; moreover, the narrated story of the other alleged group does not fit the preceding context.

Read with the surrounding verses, the question denies that their centuries-long sleep and awakening, after which they supposed they had remained only a day or part of one, was an exceptional wonder. Humanity’s continual absorption in worldly adornment, heedlessness of the hereafter, and eventual resurrection—when people will realize how briefly they remained in the world—is a perpetual divine sign of the same kind. The context also indicates that the Prophet already knew the story in outline and that revelation supplied its details; the following summary verses support this by recalling its striking features.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains that awī denotes returning to a place of settlement or security, while fitya, the irregular plural of fatā, carries a commendatory sense. Tahīʾa means preparation, and rushd is guidance to what one seeks—the opposite of ghayy and akin to hidaya.

The fāʾ in their prayer shows that, after taking refuge, they appealed to God as people stripped of all power and means. Their emphasis on mercy “from You” indicates that they sought support available only from God; alternatively, it may mean divine gifts such as guidance, an interpretation supported by the fact that their request is wholly for guidance. Their “affair” is their own perilous situation: fleeing people who persecuted believers, shed their blood, and compelled worship of other deities, they did not know what would become of them or how to save themselves. Thus, the requested rushd is the right course for deliverance. If mercy means divine support, the request for a right course is conjoined to it; if mercy means divine gifts or guidance, it is a second plea.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains “We veiled their hearing” as making the youths sleep so deeply that voices could not wake them. Al-Kashshāf takes the omitted object to be a veil; Majmaʿ al-bayān understands the expression as God’s overpowering them with sleep, an especially eloquent usage, and the commentary judges this superior to al-Zamakhsharī’s explanation. It also proposes a further allusion: God gently eased them into sleep, like a mother soothing her infant by touching its ears.

Sinīn ʿadadan qualifies ḍarabnā and means “numbered years”; ʿadad is a verbal noun meaning counting. It may alternatively be understood with an omitted muḍāf, as dhawāt ʿadad, “having numbers.” Al-Kashshāf says the description could indicate either many or few years, since before God even many are few, and al-Zajjāj relates numbering to a large quantity. Al-Mizan instead holds that what is numerous is ordinarily difficult to count, so calling the years ʿadadan implies that they were few and readily counted, as “counted dirhams” means a few dirhams in Then they sold him for a paltry price, a handful of counted dirhams (darāhima maʿdūda) . . . (12:20). This suits the context and refutes the notion that their story was the most amazing sign. The verse plainly establishes that they slept, rather than died, throughout their stay in the cave.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains that baʿth in this verse means waking from sleep, not resurrection, as the preceding context shows. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defines ḥizb as a group marked by some fierceness. He distinguishes amad, an unqualified but finite and unknown duration, from abad, which is unlimited; amad concerns an endpoint, whereas zamān may concern either a beginning or an end.

“So that We might know” denotes actual knowledge: that a thing becomes manifest and present exactly as it is in God’s sight. This Qur’anic usage is what some exegetes mean when they interpret it as manifesting what God already knows.

Their awakening had the purpose indicated by li: to show which of the two groups of the Companions of the Cave would reckon the duration of their stay. This is supported by the following account of their own disagreement: one says they remained a day or part of a day, while others answer, “Your Lord knows best how long you have tarried.” The alternative view that the two parties were the believers and unbelievers among their people, whose dispute God resolved by awakening the youths, is unlikely.

Aḥṣā is most likely a past-tense verb meaning “would reckon,” with amadan as its object and li-mā labithū qualifying the duration; mā indicates which of the two groups reckoned the length of their stay. The alternative analysis of aḥṣā as a comparative adjective, with an implied verb governing amadan, is strained.

Al-Mizan holds that verses (18:10-12) summarize the whole story as a divine and awe-inspiring sign. The youths entered the cave and prayed for mercy, safety from being forced either to worship other deities or be killed, and guidance leading to salvation. God then caused them to sleep for a limited number of years and awakened them, whereupon they became aware and disagreed about how long they had remained. These are the story’s three central points. The later verses recount them in detail and add events, including the disclosure of their secret, alluded to in “And thus did We make (people) learn of them,” beginning with “We relate to you their story with truth.”
verses.13: Al-Mizan begins the detailed account of their story. Their belief in their Lord was pleasing to Him, for otherwise it would not be attributed to them. Guidance (hudā) follows basic faith: it is an increase in belief that guides a person to all that earns God’s pleasure, as indicated by: O you who believe! Be careful of (your duty to) God and believe in His Messenger: He will give you double portions of His mercy and will make for you a light with which you will walk (57:28).
verses.14:
Al-Mizan explains that wa rabaṭnā ʿalā qulūbihim, literally binding upon their hearts, alludes to the removal of their worry and anxiety. Shaṭaṭan is an excess beyond the limit and a departure from truth, while sulṭān means evidence or proof. The verses first recount the youths’ confrontation with the idolaters, then their consultation after separating from their people and seeking refuge in the cave.

Their declaration that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and earth affirms the Oneness of the sole Lord of all things, against idolatry’s assignment of a god and lord to each class of creation. Their refusal to call upon any god besides Him also rejects the supposed higher or “meta-gods” placed above lesser gods, such as the universal intellects of the Sabians or Brahman, Shiva, and Vishnu. To invoke any created being in this way would be shaṭaṭan, for it raises a creature to the rank of the Creator.

The commentary holds that the objects of worship under discussion were not the statues themselves, but angels, jinn, and human reformers represented by statues and images; the use of a pronoun reserved for rational beings indicates this. The youths challenge their people to produce clear proof for taking such beings as gods. Their people’s rationale was that God’s sublimity made Him inaccessible to worship and that one therefore had to approach Him through noble beings near to Him. Al-Mizan replies that this argument defeats itself: neither human beings nor those close servants whom they worship can fully comprehend God. All know Him only through His names, attributes, and actions, each according to his capacity; thus all can turn to worship Him at that level of knowledge. Moreover, creating, sustaining, ruling, and managing belong to God alone, so He alone is worthy of worship.

If the idolaters cannot establish decisive proof, they speak of God without knowledge and forge a lie against Him. Such false attribution is injustice, and injustice against God is the gravest kind. By their speech, the youths showed both acknowledgment of God and insight into their religion, thereby manifesting the truth of the statement that God had increased them in guidance.

Al-Mizan reads their strengthened hearts and their standing up as indicating that they publicly proclaimed this truth rather than whispering it privately, in the face of rulers whose coercion inspired terror. Their refusal to call upon other gods further indicates that they were being forced to worship idols. “When they stood up and said” therefore most likely refers to their opposition in a king’s council or general assembly that had decreed idol worship, forbidden God’s worship, and resolved to enforce this by killing and torture. Threatened with grave danger, they left their people and were pursued from every direction. This reading supports narrations that six of them were among the king’s close confidants and rose in his council to proclaim God’s Oneness and deny partners to Him.

This does not contradict the upcoming narrations that they had concealed their faith and practised dissimulation (taqiyya): they could have kept it hidden until they suddenly declared it and departed, since continuous public profession would have led to their death. Al-Mizan also allows that qāmū may mean that they rose in support of the truth, with their declaration made privately and the instruction to separate spoken after leaving the city; alternatively, all the quoted words may have been exchanged among themselves after they had withdrawn. On either alternative, the strengthening of their hearts means that they did not fear punishment for fleeing or banishment by their people. Nevertheless, the public-confrontation explanation appears more likely.

The latter words are the second part of their dialogue, after they had left their people and the things worshipped apart from God. Iʿtizāl and taʿazzul mean separation; yanshur means unfolding; and mirfaqa, like marfiq and marfaq, denotes kind treatment. Some of them proposed hiding in the cave from the enemies of their religion. Through divine guidance, they knew that God would unfold His mercy to them and make their affair easy and beneficial, including deliverance from their people’s domination and oppression. The firm form of their statement, rather than a merely hopeful “perhaps,” indicates this recognition. The mercy and right course they expected are the same two things they later asked for in their prayer: “Our Lord! Grant us mercy from You, and provide for us a right course in our affair.”

Finally, Al-Mizan takes the exception in “what they worship save God” as discontinuous (munqaṭiʿ): God was not among the beings whom those idolaters worshipped, so He is not excluded from an otherwise included class. Some exegetes claim that the polytheists worshipped God alongside idols, or that at least some did, which would make the exception continuous (muttaṣil). The commentary rejects both claims, maintaining that such idolaters were not known to worship God with idols and that their own philosophy did not permit it.

Their declaration that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and earth affirms the Oneness of the sole Lord of all things, against idolatry’s assignment of a god and lord to each class of creation. Their refusal to call upon any god besides Him also rejects the supposed higher or “meta-gods” placed above lesser gods, such as the universal intellects of the Sabians or Brahman, Shiva, and Vishnu. To invoke any created being in this way would be shaṭaṭan, for it raises a creature to the rank of the Creator.

The commentary holds that the objects of worship under discussion were not the statues themselves, but angels, jinn, and human reformers represented by statues and images; the use of a pronoun reserved for rational beings indicates this. The youths challenge their people to produce clear proof for taking such beings as gods. Their people’s rationale was that God’s sublimity made Him inaccessible to worship and that one therefore had to approach Him through noble beings near to Him. Al-Mizan replies that this argument defeats itself: neither human beings nor those close servants whom they worship can fully comprehend God. All know Him only through His names, attributes, and actions, each according to his capacity; thus all can turn to worship Him at that level of knowledge. Moreover, creating, sustaining, ruling, and managing belong to God alone, so He alone is worthy of worship.

If the idolaters cannot establish decisive proof, they speak of God without knowledge and forge a lie against Him. Such false attribution is injustice, and injustice against God is the gravest kind. By their speech, the youths showed both acknowledgment of God and insight into their religion, thereby manifesting the truth of the statement that God had increased them in guidance.

Threatened with grave danger, they left their people and were pursued from every direction. This reading supports narrations that six of them were among the king’s close confidants and rose in his council to proclaim God’s Oneness and deny partners to Him.

verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains tazāwaru as inclining or slanting, taqriḍuhum as cutting or leaving behind, and fajwa as a wide tract or courtyard. Dhāt al-yamīn and dhāt al-shimāl denote the right- and left-hand sides. The verses portray the cave, the sleepers’ condition, and the changes around them during their long sleep. Their address in the second person is not directed to the Prophet personally, but is the common mode of addressing any listener.

Hypothetically, an observer would see the sun’s rays incline away from the cave at sunrise on the right and depart at sunset on the left, while the youths remained in a spacious part of the cave untouched by sunlight. This indicates that the cave did not face east or west, since in either case sunlight would reach it at one of those times. Rather, it lay on a north–south axis: sunlight reached its sides at sunrise and sunset but not the sleepers within. God thereby preserved them from the sun’s heat, which could have burned their skin or faded their clothes, while allowing them comfort and breeze. The indefiniteness of fajwa may imply a spacious place within the cave where the sun did not reach them.

Some exegetes, relying perhaps on the commonly held identification of the cave with one in Ephesus, say that its entrance faced north and interpret right and left from the standpoint of one entering it. Al-Mizan rejects this. The sides of a dwelling or other object with an entrance are normally determined from the position of one exiting it: its entrance is its front, and its right and left correspond to those of a person facing outward. On this basis, the verse describes a cave whose opening faced south, not north. In all events, the sleepers remained in God’s care and grace, preserved alive until their decreed lifespan ended.

The statement that this is among God’s signs is followed by the principle that the one God guides is rightly guided, while no guiding friend can be found for one whom He causes to err. Ayqāẓan, the plural of yaqīẓ or yaqẓān, means awake, and ruqūd, the plural of rāqid, means asleep. That they appeared awake while asleep suggests that their eyes were open. God turned them repeatedly from right to left and left to right so that the earth would not consume them, their clothes would not decay, and their bodily strength would not fail during their motionless stay.

Their dog lay with its forelegs extended at the waṣīd, understood as a courtyard or threshold, in the open space of the cave. This shows that it remained close to them throughout their stay. Their appearance was so dreadful that anyone unexpectedly encountering them would flee, anticipating danger, and would be filled with terror.

Al-Mizan adds that the universal second-person form in the descriptions of seeing, fleeing, and being terrified has the same non-personal force as before. The wording says that the whole person would be filled with terror, rather than merely the heart, because the dread would spread through every limb. It also properly puts flight before terror. A person flees what appears abhorrent because of anticipated danger, whether or not terror has already arisen in the heart. Flight is thus the necessary response in a fearful situation (ḥukm al-khawf), whereas terror is a distinct state of fear and agitation in the heart. Though both result from witnessing their unsettling appearance, flight more clearly indicates the threatening situation, making this order more eloquent.

verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that God roused the youths, after causing them to sleep for a long time in a remarkable state, precisely so that they would question one another and the truth of their condition would become clear. Their earlier prayer and the sleep that followed it show this to be an act of mercy and guidance. Distressed by the unbelief, tyranny, and prevalence of falsehood in their society, they had despaired that truth could prevail or that believers could enjoy religious freedom. God therefore made them sleep for years and awakened them, so that their estimate of “a day or part of a day” would reveal that centuries had passed and circumstances had changed.

Their experience also teaches that the length of time does not determine whether truth is destroyed or falsehood preserved. God has made earthly things an adornment and a trial, drawing people toward the earth and its desires to distinguish the best in deeds. A person absorbed in past events and worldly sweetness or bitterness remains like one asleep for a day; desire and worldly vanity prevent him from turning to truth. Yet death is the day on which worldly adornment no longer distracts people and the world is folded up. Al-Mizan cites ʿAlī’s reported saying: “People are asleep. When they die, they wake up.”

Accordingly, li in li-yatasāʾalū indicates purpose: they were awakened in order to ask each other how long they had remained. This accords with the earlier purpose of determining which of the two parties would reckon their stay more accurately. The view that the stated questioning merely implies the wider disclosure of the sign and divine power has no textual evidence and is contrived. Nor does the claim that their questioning was only a consequence of awakening, because calling it an insignificant consequence of so great a sign is no more suitable than calling it its purpose; in fact, their question was the real purpose explained above.

The questioner was one of the youths, apparently prompted by the heaviness remaining from deep sleep. Their answer, “a day or part of a day,” is best understood as hesitation between those two estimates, based on visible signs such as the sun, shade, light, and darkness. Such evidence does not establish a whole day without some possible error, but they were not speaking rashly or deliriously. Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that aw divides them into two groups, one saying a day and the other part of a day: the wording itself does not support it, and a single person gives the same form of answer in (2:259). In common usage, “a day” can mean slightly more than a night followed by its day.

The others’ reply, “Your Lord knows best how long you have tarried,” answers the first group; otherwise they would have said, “Our Lord knows best.” It is not merely good manners, but manifests tawḥīd: true knowledge of the essences of things and events belongs to God alone, who encompasses and witnesses everything. Human beings are veiled from what lies beyond themselves and know external things only through evidence, and only to the degree it discloses them. A monotheist must therefore attribute knowledge and every true perfection to God, claiming only what God has granted and authorized, as in (He) Taught humankind what they knew not (96:5) and They said: Glory be to You! We have no knowledge but that which You have taught us. . . (2:32).

Those who made this reply thus apparently possessed a higher degree of knowledge than those who estimated a day or part of a day. They were distinct speakers in a responsive debate, not the same people changing their formulation; this is also why they said “Your Lord,” not “Our Lord.” Their response cannot be reduced to etiquette, for etiquette is not the reckoning or guessing by either of the two parties mentioned previously. From the singular qāla and the two plural qālū forms, Al-Mizan infers that there were at least seven youths: one speaker and two groups of no fewer than three each.

Their decision to send one of themselves with their wariq, meaning dirhams or silver coin, concludes the discussion. He is to seek the city’s inhabitants for the best food, whose primary sense is good food, though it has also been interpreted as permissible (ḥalāl) or pure (ṭāhir), and to bring provision from that food. The more likely referent of minhu is the food, rather than the silver coin. He must exercise talaṭuf—gentleness and kindness—in his going, returning, and dealings, so that no quarrel or dispute exposes their situation; restricting this gentleness to his dealings alone is unsupported by the unqualified wording.

The warning that, if the people yaẓharū ʿalaykum, they will stone the youths or return them to their religion explains this caution. Although ẓahara ʿalā can mean finding out about something or prevailing over it, the context most comprehensively means becoming familiar with them and discovering their hiding place, which would enable the powerful townspeople to overcome them. Stoning them to death, the most repulsive form of killing, indicates that the whole city opposed their religion and would join in killing them.

The phrase aw yuʿidūkum fī millatihim likely means forcing them back into their religion, not merely returning them to it; its use of fī rather than ilā supports this. Since the youths had openly denounced that religion as a grievous word and a lie against God, their people would not accept a mere outward declaration or empty conformity. They would compel them to participate in idolatry and all its rites, while barring them from God’s religious practices and from speaking the truth.

Al-Mizan distinguishes this case from one in which a believer is genuinely trapped among unbelievers in pagan lands (bilād al-kufr). Such a compelled person may retain faith in his heart while denying it verbally, as indicated by . . . not he who is compelled while his heart is at rest on account of faith. . . (16:106),and . . . but you should guard yourselves against them, guarding carefully. . . (3:28). But a person who has escaped and is free to believe and act, then throws himself into the danger of misguidance and becomes trapped where he cannot profess truth or discharge religious and human duties, deprives himself of happiness and will never succeed. This is why the consequence is categorical, as in Surely (as for) those whom the angels cause to die while they are unjust to their souls, they shall say: In what state were you? They shall say: We were weak in the earth. They shall say: Was not God’s earth spacious, so that you should have migrated therein? So these it is whose abode is hell, and it is an evil resort (4:97).

The objection that coerced dissimulation should be forgiven is answered by the fact that, if they exposed themselves and were consequently forced back, they would willingly have caused the circumstance and would not be excused. Al-Mizan rejects three other answers: that coercion might lead Satan to make disbelief seem good, since this would warrant only fear of failure rather than the categorical statement; that “forcing back” means attempted persuasion, which the context does not support; and that taqiyya was then absolutely forbidden, for which there is no evidence.

The reported exchange displays their love for one another for God’s sake, religious brotherhood, equality, mutual counsel, and kindness. “Send one of you” is a proposal addressed equally to them all, not an imperious command to a named individual, and “this silver coin of yours” makes the coin common to them all. Their instructions concerning food and gentleness, and their warning about capture, are advice meant to preserve their lives and religious practice.

Finally, the possessive construction and demonstrative in bi wariqikum hādhihi suggest that this particular coin had a special significance. Al-Mizan considers it possible that the coin exposed their secret: when the messenger paid with it, it was recognized as having been minted three centuries earlier. Apart from this expression, the verses give no other clue as to how their situation became known.

verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that wa kadhālika aʿtharnā ʿalayhīm means that God caused people to come upon the Companions of the Cave unexpectedly, not that they sought them out. As al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān notes, ʿathara literally denotes stumbling and is metaphorically used for discovering something accidentally. The comparison with “And thus did We rouse them” means that, just as God caused the youths to be forgotten, then awakened them for a purpose, He caused people to discover them. The implied object of aʿtharnā is the people, and “God’s promise” here means the Resurrection; the assertion that there is no doubt about the Hour explains and reinforces this promise.

The commentary’s principal reading is that people were disputing about resurrection when God made them witness the youths, so that they would know resurrection to be true and the Hour unquestionable. An alternative reading makes their discovery an additional event alongside the existing dispute. Their long sleep and awakening are themselves evidence for resurrection: their souls had been removed from their bodies, sensation and bodily functions had ceased, yet their bodies, clothing, and appearance did not decay or change. This resembles death, when souls leave bodies, and resurrection, when they return to them. Both the youths’ awakening after three centuries and the resurrection are miraculous; the obstacle is people’s difficulty in believing them, not evidence against them.

According to the commentary, the event occurred amid a disagreement between monotheists, who held that the soul leaves the body at death and returns to it at resurrection, and polytheists, who denied resurrection. The latter held that the soul permanently separates from the body and may instead have believed in reincarnation. The incident thus served as a divine sign that removed doubt about resurrection through an analogous occurrence. The youths died only hours after awakening—long enough for people to learn, gather, and verify their story—and this made belief in resurrection firmer.

Al-Mizan also considers a second grammatical interpretation of “When they disputed among themselves about their affair.” On this reading, the first two plural pronouns refer to the people, while “their affair” refers to the Companions of the Cave: after discovering them and recognizing the truth of resurrection, people disputed about whether the youths were asleep or dead and whether they should be buried or left in the cave. An objection is that this makes the dispute occur after the discovery and after certainty about the Hour, whereas the original dispute about resurrection preceded both. The response is that these are two separate disputes: the earlier dispute concerned resurrection, while the later one concerned the youths themselves.

The commentary nevertheless prefers the first interpretation. It holds that the people who said, “Erect an edifice over them, their Lord knows them best,” were polytheists. Their proposed structure would cover and conceal the youths, cutting people off from them. Although the sign pointed clearly to resurrection, they remained uncertain and sought to leave the matter hidden, saying “Their Lord knows them best.” By contrast, the monotheists recognized the sign and replied, “We will certainly raise a masjid over them,” where God would be remembered and the youths commemorated. The wording “their Lord,” rather than “our Lord,” and the opposition between an enclosing edifice and a masjid support this preferred reading.

The preceding and following clauses allude, in Al-Mizan’s reconstruction, to the fuller event: when the youths’ messenger entered the city, three hundred years had passed and monotheism had replaced the earlier prevailing polytheism without his knowledge. His old coin exposed his secret; people spread the news and hurried to the cave, the divine proof was established, and God then took the youths to Himself. The statement “Their Lord knows them best” further suggests a division among the gathered people: some recognized the truth, while others remained indecisive and dissatisfied with it.

“Those who prevailed in their affair” are most plausibly the monotheists, who prevailed through the sign establishing resurrection. Their proposed masjid is specifically a place of prostration and remembrance of God, not merely a maʿbad, a general place of worship. Other possibilities—that those who prevailed were the king and his aides, people holding authority, or the youths’ relatives—are mentioned, but the relatives interpretation is dismissed as especially absurd. The verse has generated innumerable permutations among exegetes because of its vocabulary, pronouns, and clauses; Al-Mizan confines itself to readings warranted by the context.

On (18:22), Al-Mizan says that the verse records three circulating estimates of the Companions’ number: three with their dog as the fourth, five with their dog as the sixth, and seven with their dog as the eighth. “Making conjectures at what is unknown” (rajman bi-l-ghayb) applies to both the first and second estimates; otherwise the arrangement of the statements would not fit. The third estimate is stated without a rebuke, which indicates that seven, with the dog as the eighth, is the sound view. The earlier wording of the youths’ conversation likewise indicates, or at least strongly suggests, that they numbered no fewer than seven.

Rajm originally means stoning. Rajman bi-l-ghayb therefore portrays unsupported claims as stones thrown at an unseen target: the speaker does not know whether the claim will strike truth or falsehood. The alternative interpretation, that it means believing in the unseen, is unlikely. The ordered progression—three and a fourth, five and a sixth, seven and an eighth—is also part of the verse’s expressive beauty.

The conjunction wa appears only in “seven, and the eighth of them is their dog.” Al-Kashshāf explains that each number is the predicate of an omitted subject and that the following phrase describes it; wa can introduce such a descriptive phrase in order to make its attachment definite and firm. Al-Mizan accordingly takes the conjunction to show that the final statement was made with knowledge and confidence, unlike the preceding conjectures. This is supported by the fact that the first two opinions are followed by rajman bi-l-ghayb, while the third is followed by “none knows them but a few.” Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said, “When the ‘and’ (wa) appeared, the counting stopped,” meaning that seven and their dog as the eighth was decisively established. Majmaʿ al-bayān, reporting Abū ʿAlī l-Fārisī, adds that grammarians do not accept the claim that wa is uniquely associated with the number eight.

The command, “Say: My Lord knows best their number,” ends speculative discussion. “None knows them but a few” implies that a few did know; Al-Mizan considers it likely that they were among the People of the Book. The future forms “some will say” show that all three opinions were current around the time of revelation, or in the near future relative to the narrated event.

Finally, the Prophet is told not to dispute over them except with an outward contention and not to seek a definitive answer from those disputing. Miryah is a more particular kind of uncertainty than shakk, and mumārāt is persistent contention over what is uncertain. “Outward contention” may mean restricting discussion to the manifest Qur’anic account without probing deeply, insulting opponents, or engaging their unsupported details; it may also mean using a clear proof that eliminates their argument. Since God has informed the Prophet of their story, he is to rely on that disclosure rather than pursue further speculative claims.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that wa kadhālika aʿtharnā ʿalayhīm means that God caused people to come upon the Companions of the Cave unexpectedly, not that they sought them out. As al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān notes, ʿathara literally denotes stumbling and is metaphorically used for discovering something accidentally. The comparison with “And thus did We rouse them” means that, just as God caused the youths to be forgotten, then awakened them for a purpose, He caused people to discover them. The implied object of aʿtharnā is the people, and “God’s promise” here means the Resurrection; the assertion that there is no doubt about the Hour explains and reinforces this promise.

The commentary’s principal reading is that people were disputing about resurrection when God made them witness the youths, so that they would know resurrection to be true and the Hour unquestionable. An alternative reading makes their discovery an additional event alongside the existing dispute. Their long sleep and awakening are themselves evidence for resurrection: their souls had been removed from their bodies, sensation and bodily functions had ceased, yet their bodies, clothing, and appearance did not decay or change. This resembles death, when souls leave bodies, and resurrection, when they return to them. Both the youths’ awakening after three centuries and the resurrection are miraculous; the obstacle is people’s difficulty in believing them, not evidence against them.

According to the commentary, the event occurred amid a disagreement between monotheists, who held that the soul leaves the body at death and returns to it at resurrection, and polytheists, who denied resurrection. The latter held that the soul permanently separates from the body and may instead have believed in reincarnation. The incident thus served as a divine sign that removed doubt about resurrection through an analogous occurrence. The youths died only hours after awakening—long enough for people to learn, gather, and verify their story—and this made belief in resurrection firmer.

Al-Mizan also considers a second grammatical interpretation of “When they disputed among themselves about their affair.” On this reading, the first two plural pronouns refer to the people, while “their affair” refers to the Companions of the Cave: after discovering them and recognizing the truth of resurrection, people disputed about whether the youths were asleep or dead and whether they should be buried or left in the cave. An objection is that this makes the dispute occur after the discovery and after certainty about the Hour, whereas the original dispute about resurrection preceded both. The response is that these are two separate disputes: the earlier dispute concerned resurrection, while the later one concerned the youths themselves.

The commentary nevertheless prefers the first interpretation. It holds that the people who said, “Erect an edifice over them, their Lord knows them best,” were polytheists. Their proposed structure would cover and conceal the youths, cutting people off from them. Although the sign pointed clearly to resurrection, they remained uncertain and sought to leave the matter hidden, saying “Their Lord knows them best.” By contrast, the monotheists recognized the sign and replied, “We will certainly raise a masjid over them,” where God would be remembered and the youths commemorated. The wording “their Lord,” rather than “our Lord,” and the opposition between an enclosing edifice and a masjid support this preferred reading.

The preceding and following clauses allude, in Al-Mizan’s reconstruction, to the fuller event: when the youths’ messenger entered the city, three hundred years had passed and monotheism had replaced the earlier prevailing polytheism without his knowledge. His old coin exposed his secret; people spread the news and hurried to the cave, the divine proof was established, and God then took the youths to Himself. The statement “Their Lord knows them best” further suggests a division among the gathered people: some recognized the truth, while others remained indecisive and dissatisfied with it.

“Those who prevailed in their affair” are most plausibly the monotheists, who prevailed through the sign establishing resurrection. Their proposed masjid is specifically a place of prostration and remembrance of God, not merely a maʿbad, a general place of worship. Other possibilities—that those who prevailed were the king and his aides, people holding authority, or the youths’ relatives—are mentioned, but the relatives interpretation is dismissed as especially absurd. The verse has generated innumerable permutations among exegetes because of its vocabulary, pronouns, and clauses; Al-Mizan confines itself to readings warranted by the context.

On (18:22), Al-Mizan says that the verse records three circulating estimates of the Companions’ number: three with their dog as the fourth, five with their dog as the sixth, and seven with their dog as the eighth. “Making conjectures at what is unknown” (rajman bi-l-ghayb) applies to both the first and second estimates; otherwise the arrangement of the statements would not fit. The third estimate is stated without a rebuke, which indicates that seven, with the dog as the eighth, is the sound view. The earlier wording of the youths’ conversation likewise indicates, or at least strongly suggests, that they numbered no fewer than seven.

Rajm originally means stoning. Rajman bi-l-ghayb therefore portrays unsupported claims as stones thrown at an unseen target: the speaker does not know whether the claim will strike truth or falsehood. The alternative interpretation, that it means believing in the unseen, is unlikely. The ordered progression—three and a fourth, five and a sixth, seven and an eighth—is also part of the verse’s expressive beauty.

The conjunction wa appears only in “seven, and the eighth of them is their dog.” Al-Kashshāf explains that each number is the predicate of an omitted subject and that the following phrase describes it; wa can introduce such a descriptive phrase in order to make its attachment definite and firm. Al-Mizan accordingly takes the conjunction to show that the final statement was made with knowledge and confidence, unlike the preceding conjectures. This is supported by the fact that the first two opinions are followed by rajman bi-l-ghayb, while the third is followed by “none knows them but a few.” Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said, “When the ‘and’ (wa) appeared, the counting stopped,” meaning that seven and their dog as the eighth was decisively established. Majmaʿ al-bayān, reporting Abū ʿAlī l-Fārisī, adds that grammarians do not accept the claim that wa is uniquely associated with the number eight.

The command, “Say: My Lord knows best their number,” ends speculative discussion. “None knows them but a few” implies that a few did know; Al-Mizan considers it likely that they were among the People of the Book. The future forms “some will say” show that all three opinions were current around the time of revelation, or in the near future relative to the narrated event.

Finally, the Prophet is told not to dispute over them except with an outward contention and not to seek a definitive answer from those disputing. Miryah is a more particular kind of uncertainty than shakk, and mumārāt is persistent contention over what is uncertain. “Outward contention” may mean restricting discussion to the manifest Qur’anic account without probing deeply, insulting opponents, or engaging their unsupported details; it may also mean using a clear proof that eliminates their argument. Since God has informed the Prophet of their story, he is to rely on that disclosure rather than pursue further speculative claims.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan holds that, whether addressed solely to the Prophet or also to others, the verse concerns anyone who attributes a present or future act to himself. The Qur’an teaches that nothing—neither essences nor causes and effects—belongs independently to anyone but God. He alone decides concerning all things, and no one possesses or controls anything except insofar as He grants possession and control. Agents, means, and natural causes are not self-sufficient in producing effects: they act only because God gives them ability, removes impediments, and does not will the contrary. This is His permission (idhn), and every action of every agent is contingent on it.

Accordingly, one who knows God’s true status should not regard himself as an independent cause of his acts. His strength, possession, and control are from God; when he resolves on an act, he should do so while trusting in God, and when he promises or announces a future act, he should qualify it by God’s permission or by the proviso that God may will otherwise. The preceding discussion of God’s oneness, divinity, lordship, and the transience of earthly adornment reinforces this meaning. Human deeds, being among what is on earth, are also an adornment and a test, though people suppose that they own them.

The verse does not prohibit attributing an act to its human agent as such, for the Qur’an itself attributes acts to the Prophet and to other people. It rejects only attributing acts to an agent as independent of God’s will and permission. Grammatically, Al-Mizan understands “unless God pleases” through a bāʾ of concomitance (bāʾ al-mulābasa), with an exception extending over every circumstance and time: one must not say unconditionally, “I will do it tomorrow,” but say it as dependent upon God’s will—if He allows it, or unless He wills otherwise.

Al-Mizan rejects several other explanations. Al-Akhfash’s view, which supplies an omitted “say” and makes the meaning “unless you say, ‘God willing,’” treats the phrase as training people not to speak categorically lest an impediment make them lie or break an oath; the commentary regards this ellipsis as contrived and as altering the meaning. Another view takes God’s will as legislative will (irāda tashrīʿiyya), so that the prohibition applies only to intending acts of obedience, not permissible acts. Al-Mizan rejects this because there is no evidence that mashiʾa is used in that sense; rather, Qur’anic usage establishes the dependence of acts on God’s creational will, as in “If God pleases (in shāʾ Allāh).” It further identifies the view with Muʿtazilī fundamentals, according to which God’s will concerning servants’ acts is only legislative and attached to obedience, a proposition it says reason and textual evidence disprove.

A third interpretation, also associated with the Muʿtazilīs, makes the exception refer to doing rather than saying: a servant acts independently unless God produces a stronger impediment. Al-Mizan answers that an exception can indeed refer to doing, as it does elsewhere in the Qur’an; therefore there is no reason to exclude this grammatical possibility, and the verse should instead be read consistently with its proper sense. A fourth view makes the meaning, “Do not say it unless God permits you to say it.” It is rejected because it must infer an unexpressed idea of telling or permission without textual evidence, thereby imposing an unknown obligation. A fifth makes the exception mean “ever,” so that one must never say such a thing. This conflicts with Qur’anic verses that attribute past and future acts to the Prophet and others, command them to do so, and with the command immediately following to remember God when one forgets.

The connection with the preceding command shows that “when you forget” means forgetting to say “God willing,” not forgetting God generally or forgetting any matter. Remembering the Lord means recalling the divine status which grounds the exception: God attends to every soul through what it earns, grants people their possession and ability, and makes them controllers only of what He has placed under their control. Thus, when one remembers having omitted “God willing,” he should remember God in a way that surrenders power and authority to Him and qualifies acts by His permission and will.

Because the command to remember God is unrestricted, it is not confined to a particular formula. One may append “unless God pleases” before finishing the statement, repeat the statement with that acknowledgment, or, after a short or long interval, refer back to the earlier statement and acknowledge its dependence on God’s will. Some narrations report that when these verses were revealed, the Prophet said, “God willing,” or remembered God through seeking forgiveness or something similar. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the claims that the verse stands independently and concerns forgetting God or anything whatsoever, and that remembrance is exclusively uttering “unless God pleases,” exclusively seeking forgiveness, or merely regretting one’s negligence.

Finally, “Maybe my Lord will guide me to a nearer course to the right than this” continues the same instruction. “This” (hādhā) refers to remembering after having forgotten; the hoped-for guidance is to something nearer to right than forgetting and then remembering—namely, perpetual remembrance without forgetfulness. Repeatedly recalling what one forgot is itself a means toward constant remembrance. Al-Mizan rejects readings that make “this” refer to the reports of the Companions of the Cave, to the forgotten object itself, or make the final clause an explanatory command to repent after any kind of forgetfulness, since all rest on severing the verse from its context or on taking forgetting in the unrestricted sense.

verses.25:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse directly states the duration of the Companions’ sleep: three hundred years, with nine added. It clarifies the earlier vague reference to “numbered years in the cave.” The subsequent command, Say: God knows best how long they remained, does not dispute the stated number; together with the commands to recite the revelation and declare that truth is from God, and with the absence of any alternative figure, it confirms it, much as “My Lord knows best their number” confirms a number already given.

The commentary rejects the claims that the duration is quoted from the People of the Book and then answered by Say: God knows best how long they remained, or that “they added (another) nine” means the People of the Book added nine years to the true figure. Reports from the People of the Book instead give two hundred years or less, not three hundred, let alone three hundred and nine.

Grammatically, sinīn is not the specifying complement of the number, for that would require thalatha miʾatin sana; it is in apposition to thalāthamiʾatin and echoes sinīna ʿadadan. Perhaps using sinīn rather than sana presents the stay as long from the human perspective, while “they added (another) nine” juxtaposes three hundred years with a further nine. This does not conflict with the earlier presentation of the years as few: there the purpose was to show that the cave’s sign was not astonishing beside God’s making all earthly things an embellishment, whereas here the long sojourn is a divine sign and proof against deniers of resurrection. The period is slight in God’s perspective but long in ours.

The three hundred plus nine are lunar years: three hundred solar years differ from three hundred lunar years by about nine years, and Qur’anic sana denotes the lunar year measured by months beginning with the new moon, as used in the Islamic shariah. Al-Tafsīr al-kabīr strongly objects that the figures are not exact and challenges a report attributed to ʿAlī on this matter, but the difference between three hundred solar years and three hundred and nine lunar years is less than three months; such approximation is common in speech.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse continues the account of the Companions of the Cave, answering people’s dispute over their stay by affirming that God’s account is indubitably true. The command, “Say: God knows best how long they remained,” directs the Prophet to settle their uncertainty by God’s superior knowledge of them and their circumstances.

“To Him (lahu) belong the unseen things of the heavens and the earth” gives the first proof: lahu denotes God’s exclusive and real possession of all that is unseen, so nothing escapes Him, even if it escapes those in heaven and earth. Since the length of their stay is among the unseen, and God’s sight and hearing are perfect, He necessarily knows it best. “How clear His sight” (abṣar) and “how clear His hearing” (asmiʿ) are exclamations of the perfection of these attributes; they add that He saw their condition and heard what they said. The commentary rejects the view that lahu means only that God alone knows the unseen, from which knowledge of all else is inferred: the exclamations most likely introduce a further point rather than repeat the preceding one, and lahu literally signifies complete possession, not merely knowledge.

“There is none to be a guardian for them besides Him, and He does not make anyone His associate in His judgment” supplies a second proof, specific to them. It denies every other guardianship, whether independent of God or delegated by Him. The verbal form “He does not make” also shows that the first clause excludes both kinds of guardianship. God appoints no associate to rule or judge on His behalf as earthly rulers entrust governors with affairs independently of their own knowledge. Thus, because He alone is their guardian and Himself judges them, He knows their stay better than anyone. The pronoun in lahum most appropriately refers to the Companions of the Cave, though it may refer to everything in the heavens and earth. The two proofs are left unconnected by a conjunction because they serve different aims.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that multaḥad, “refuge,” derives from iltiḥād, inclining. “The Book of your Lord” may mean the Qur’an or the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), the latter fitting the statement that none can alter God’s words.

The command to recite is linked to the preceding consolation not to destroy oneself in grief over unbelievers. The Prophet is to recite the revealed Book because God’s words are true and firm and cannot be altered, and because there is no refuge besides Him. These are two reasons for the command; although the absence of refuge applies to everyone, the Prophet is directly addressed.

Alternatively, the lack of refuge is especially fitting for a Messenger, who can turn only to the One who sent him. On this reading, the unalterability of God’s words requires him to convey the divine communications entrusted to him. This is supported by: Say: Surely no one can protect me against God, nor can I find besides Him any place of refuge: (It is) only a delivering (of communications) from God and His messages; and whoever disobeys God and His Messenger surely he shall have the fire of hell to abide therein for a long time (72:22–23).
verses.28:
Al-Mizan explains ṣabr as restraining oneself under hardship from what reason and religious law require one to avoid. The Prophet is commanded to remain with those who continually call on their Lord, for “morning and evening” is a metonymy for persistent, uninterrupted devotion, not merely prayer at the day’s beginning and end or the prescribed daily prayers.

Seeking God’s “countenance” means seeking Him through His most beautiful names and supreme attributes, by which people call on and worship Him; His essence itself cannot be reached. When the sought attributes concern His acts, such as mercy, pleasure, favor, and grace, the worshipper seeks to be their recipient. When they concern His essence rather than His acts, such as knowledge, power, magnificence, and might, he seeks nearness by taking the posture these attributes demand: humility, weakness, and need before divine perfection. Thus wajh should not be reduced to metaphorical “pleasure” or pleasing obedience, to the essence through an implied word, or merely to tawajjuh, turning toward God and seeking nearness.

The prohibition against letting one’s eyes pass beyond such believers means not overlooking or missing them in desire for worldly adornment. God’s making a heart heedless of His remembrance is a punitive abandonment following stubborn opposition to truth: He makes such people stray by causing them to forget His remembrance. This does not establish that God initially compels unbelief or disobedience; coercion imposed as punishment does not negate free choice, unlike initial coercion. Hence contrived reinterpretations of “whose heart We have made heedless” are unnecessary.

Finally, furuṭ means exceeding what is right and departing from it. Following desire and exceeding due bounds are effects that explain the heart’s heedlessness.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan places this command among the Prophet’s duties in the face of persistent unbelief: rather than grieve, he must recite revelation, remain with the poor believers, and tell the unbelievers that the truth is from their Lord. He need not do more than convey and persuade; belief benefits God not at all, nor does disbelief harm Him, while reward and punishment belong to those who choose.

“Whoever wills—let him believe; and whoever wills—let him disbelieve” addresses the Prophet, rather than continuing the speech he is commanded to deliver. Though phrased as a choice, it is in reality a threat, clarified by the prepared Fire. The Prophet is not commanded to force or pester them, since the consequences God has prepared sufficiently induce or deter them; they choose which outcome to face.

The Fire’s surādiq is an enclosing encampment or a covering wound around it. Muhl is coagulated oil, though it is also said to be molten brass, and murtafaq denotes a place of resting on one’s elbow. The use of ẓulm rather than kufr indicates that this punishment concerns those genuinely iniquitous: those who “hinder (people) from God’s way and seek to make it crooked, and they are disbelievers in the hereafter (7:45).”
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse states the believers’ reward for faith joined to good works. Saying, “We do not waste,” rather than simply announcing a prepared reward, expresses God’s special care and gratitude: believers who do good will receive their reward in full.

Because punishment is attached to iniquity while reward is attached to belief and good action, the verse indicates that faith without good works receives no reward; it may even suggest that such faith counts as iniquity.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains that ʿAdn means perpetuity, so jannātu ʿadnin are gardens of perpetuity. Asāwir denotes bracelets; sundus is fine silk, istabraq thick silk brocade, and arāʾik couches. The verse’s promise of rivers, gold bracelets, green silk garments, and reclining on couches is otherwise clear.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains this as a parable for people engrossed in worldly adornment and turned away from God’s remembrance, showing that their attachment is to an unreal mirage. Some exegetes take the story as hypothetical, while others regard it as historical and relate differing accounts; the described arrangement of two vineyards, surrounding palms, and cultivated land between them supports its being a real story.

The two gardens of grapes (aʿnab) are vineyards, since trees may be named for their fruit. Wa ḥafafnāhumā bi nakhl means that both were surrounded with palms, while the fields lay between the two gardens, joining the cultivated area and making it productive.
verses.33: Al-Mizan explains that atat ukulahā means that the vines and palms bore their fruit. Wa lam taẓlim minhu shayʾan means the gardens suffered no failure or loss in their yield, but produced all they were capable of producing. The river gushing between them supplied their irrigation abundantly and with ease.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan takes thamar primarily to mean the man’s various kinds of wealth, though it may mean that the palms bore much fruit, or that he possessed property beyond the gardens. The latter sense is especially straightforward if the preceding description means that the gardens had reached the season of full fruitfulness. Muḥāwara is a spoken exchange, and nafar denotes adherents; here it most suitably means his children and servants, since the companion later speaks of wealth and children.

The man’s boast that he possessed greater wealth and more followers reveals a false belief that he could dispose freely of what he had and that the visible causes producing effects operated independently. Although he did possess and control these things, he forgot that God had placed them in his possession, and that wealth and children are worldly adornments and a test. Relying on apparent causes (al-asbāb al-ẓāhira) as autonomous is polytheism. He consequently regarded his possessions as an honor peculiar to himself, became conceited, and treated his companion arrogantly.

The Qur’an accordingly says that God made one man two gardens, whereas the man says, “I have” greater wealth and followers: he sees only himself and forgets the Lord who entrusted him with property and strengthened him with dependents. His claim resembles Qārūn’s, “He said: I have only been given this on account of the knowledge I have . . . (28:78).” It asserts a personal claim to distinction and entitlement and leads to his later reliance on his garden’s permanence and his doubt that the Hour will come.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains that the singular janna may refer generically to the gardens, or to the fact that he could enter them only one at a time. Al-Kashshāf offers a further explanation, which the commentary approves: the garden was the man’s only “heaven”; he would have no share in the heaven promised to believers.

His being unjust to himself consists in the arrogance, self-conceit, and association of partners with God displayed in his boast of superior wealth and followers. By forgetting God and relying on apparent causes, he commits one of the gravest perils. His words, “I do not think that this will ever perish,” concern the garden and use “not thinking” rhetorically: its destruction appears so impossible to him that it never enters his mind. He is therefore certain that it will endure.

This expresses a broader human condition. Hearts cling not to what they expect to vanish but to what appears enduring. When worldly prosperity comes, a person becomes absorbed in its adornments, hopes endlessly, and cannot imagine the loss of blessings or their means; when it departs, he may likewise imagine that hardship will last forever. God has made this attachment to ephemeral adornments a trial. Those who turn from their Lord’s remembrance become engrossed in the present and apparent causes, forget their transience, and ignore reason’s warning that time, means, pleasures, and life itself will end.

Thus worldly people follow whim and impulsive judgment against reason, treating apparent causes as permanent and worldly adornments as eternal. The man says, “I do not think,” rather than directly asserting permanence, because this is the disposition behind his words. The same conviction makes the Hour seem remote and produces doubt about resurrection.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan says that the man’s claim that, even if returned to his Lord, he would find something better rests on self-importance and a supposed entitlement to happiness without work. He assumes that his own nobility guarantees him a better return, rather than saying that God will grant it. His delusion is intensified by the oath-like force of wa la in rudidtu and the emphatic la ajidanna; he says, “I am returned” and “I will most certainly find,” not that his Lord returns or gives him something.

The following four verses answer two claims contained in his words: first, that he, his wealth, and his followers stand independent of God’s control; second, that he is superior to his companion because of his greater wealth and followers. “Do you disbelieve in Him . . . save in God” refutes the first, and “If you consider me to be inferior . . . find it” refutes the second.

The repetition that the companion disputed with him shows that faith preserved the companion’s composure and courtesy. He answered gently and avoided language that would seem malicious or offensive: unlike the garden, he did not explicitly foretell disaster for the man’s son, but only implied the garden’s possible devastation and the sinking of its water.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan holds that the companion’s question is a rhetorical condemnation of associating partners with God through the claim that oneself and apparent causes are autonomous. The man’s regarding the Hour as remote and doubting it is one aspect of this association.

The commentary rejects al-Kashshāf’s view that the man is simply an unbeliever who denies God’s blessings because he doubts resurrection. His later retraction denies associating partners with God, not merely disbelief in resurrection. Nor is he a polytheist in the sense of an idolater: by calling God “my Lord,” he acknowledges what idolatry would not allow, for idolaters make Him one lord and god among many. He does not explicitly deny resurrection, but doubts it and puts it out of mind as remote; otherwise he would have said, “And if I were to be returned” (wa law rudidtu), rather than, “If I am returned to my Lord” (wa la in rudidtu ilā rabbī).

His evil lies in forgetting his Lord and assigning autonomous dominion and disposal to himself and visible causes. This denies God’s Lordship in reality, whatever one professes orally. Al-Zamakhsharī aptly observes that, even when many wealthy Muslims do not say that their wealth will never perish, their conduct displays the same belief.

By recalling that the man was created from dust and then a small seed before becoming a complete man, the believer refutes his supposed independence. Everything beyond man’s elemental origin—his humanity, knowledge, life, capacity, power, and ability to employ created causes—is God’s gift. It is placed in human possession without ceasing to belong to God or becoming detached from Him. A human being possesses these qualities only by God’s will and cannot be independent in himself, his attributes and effects, or any cause in the universe.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains that the prevalent reading lakinnā, “but as for me,” derives from lakin anā through omission and merger. The believer’s repeated use of rabbī in “I do not associate anyone with my Lord,” rather than merely saying “with Him,” gives the reason for his refusal: because God is his Lord, no one may be associated with Him. This is the believer’s declaration against the claim made by his unbelieving companion.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains that the believer reproaches his companion for saying, “I do not think that this will ever perish,” when he should have said, “It is as God has pleased; there is no power save in God.” Every blessing must be referred to God’s will, and all power belongs to Him. “It is as God has pleased” most suitably means, in this context, that the matter is as God has willed, though it may also mean “whatever God pleases will be” or, conditionally, “whatever God pleases, is.” “There is no power save in God” means that every power manifested through creatures subsists through Him and does not make them independent; “the power is wholly God’s . . . (2:165).”

The believer then answers the man’s boast of superior wealth and children. Since God granted him those things and directs affairs by His will and power, he has no ground for pride. God may give the believer something better, or reverse their conditions by destroying the other’s garden: He may send a ḥusbān from heaven, leaving it smooth, bare ground, or cause its water to sink so deeply that it cannot be recovered. Ḥusbān conveys a destructive shower or barrage, while zalaq is smooth ground without vegetation and ghawran is water sunk into the earth. Tarani, “you see me,” likely means “you consider me,” though it may retain its literal sense.
