verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains uḥīṭa, “his wealth was destroyed,” as a figure of speech for ruin: to be surrounded like an enemy is to be cut off from all assistance. Yuqallibu kaffayhi, “wringing his hands,” likewise signifies regret. The garden’s having fallen upon its roofs depicts complete destruction, as roofs fall first and walls then collapse over them.

His regret for what he spent on the ruined garden culminates in wishing that he had not associated anyone with his Lord. That is, he wishes he had not clung to, relied upon, and treated as autonomous the means that failed him, but had referred the whole matter to God. His wealth, or its fruit, had perished, and the causes in which he trusted—himself included—proved useless.
verses.43: Al-Mizan explains fiʾa as a host and muntaṣiran as being unassailable or able to defend oneself. The sequence from the companion’s reply through the man’s destruction practically demonstrates the error of thinking that the world and its adornments will last. The ruin of his wealth and garden disproves his confidence in their permanence, while his lack of any host besides God and his inability to defend himself disprove his reliance on wealth, followers, and apparent causes.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan notes that walāya and the alternative reading wilāya have the same meaning; the proposed distinction between assistance and sovereignty is unestablished. Although some exegetes take “Here” to mean the moment when the man’s wealth was destroyed and understand walāya as God’s assistance when all other means fail, the commentary judges this insufficient for the passage’s purpose.

The verses are meant to show that everything belongs to God and that He creates and directs all things, while other things are a mirage and a worldly trial. The designation “God’s, the True One,” and the statement that He is best in reward and requital indicate, though God knows best, that walāya means directorial ownership (mālikiyya al-tadbīr), as in: Only God is your walī, and His Messenger . . . (5:55).

When calamity comes and causes fail, it becomes clear that God alone directs humanity and all things because He alone is true. Apparent causes have no independent efficacy; they possess only the effect God permits and grants them. Human autonomy is merely nominal and is true only through God, whereas God is true in His Essence, autonomous and self-sufficient.

God gives a real and lasting reward to those who serve Him. The causes to which people cling give only a false, temporary reward, and even that occurs by God’s permission. Such causes are finite, changing worldly embellishments that eventually vanish. Since a person must rely on one to whom direction and well-being are attributed, his Lord is better than all else in reward and requital. The interpretation that “Here” refers to the Day of Resurrection, and thus to reward and punishment on that Day, is not supported by the context.
verses.45: Al-Mizan describes this as the second parable of worldly life and its swiftly vanishing adornment. It is like rain sent from the sky, through which the earth’s vegetation becomes richly intermingled and beautiful, but then becomes fragile, broken pieces scattered by the winds. The wording indicates rain’s predominance in producing the vegetation; other waters are not mentioned because rain is their source. God has power over all things, including this flourishing and its destruction.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan presents the verse as the conclusion of the parable: wealth and children, though hearts cling to them and hope to profit through them, quickly pass away and fail to fulfill most of what people expect from them. They are worldly adornments, whereas al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt means good works. Human deeds are recorded with God and therefore abide; when they are good, they are abiding good. They bring a better reward and a better hope, since the mercy and honor expected from God through them surpass worldly adornments, whose promises are mostly false and whose fulfilled hopes are still beguilement and delusion.

Narrations from the Prophet transmitted by both Sunnī and Shī‘ah sources, and narrations from the Imams of the People of the Household transmitted by the Shia, interpret al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt as the four glorifications (al-tasbīḥāt al-arbaʿ): subḥān Allāh (glory be to God), al-ḥamdu li-llāh (praise be to God), lā ilāha illā Allāh (there is no god but God), and Allāhu akbar (God is too great to be described). Reports also apply it to prayer or love for the People of the Household; these are allegorical interpretations and applications of the Qur’an to particular instances.
verses.47: Al-Mizan takes the opening phrase as implying, “Remember the day.” The mountains’ passing away means their leaving their places, as elsewhere they are described as loose sand, loosened wool, scattered dust, or a mirage. Their removal makes the earth a completely level, unobstructed plain, with no part concealed from another; it may also allude to, And the earth shall beam with the light of its Lord . . . (39:69). God’s gathering of humanity leaves out no one at all.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan holds that the plural pronouns refer to polytheists: people attached to themselves, worldly adornment, and apparent causes as though these would last forever. Such attachment severs them from their Lord, entails denial of return to Him, and makes them indifferent to His pleasure and wrath. When the test ends, causes are cut off, hopes vanish, and the world is laid bare; they remain only with their Lord, themselves, and the recorded book of their deeds.

They are brought before “your Lord” in a single row for decisive judgment, without any worldly rank based on lineage, wealth, social position, mastery, or servitude. The wording indicates both that they have no alternative to returning to Him and that they receive no honor there; deeds alone distinguish people. Then they recognize God as the manifest truth and see that their alleged deities, worldly embellishments, supposed independence, and relied-upon causes were illusions that could not replace God. The verse selects fundamental stages of the full account: their presentation, their arrival as first created, their false assumption, and the placement of the book.

“Now certainly you have come to Us as We created you at first” is direct divine speech exposing the error of allowing worldly adornment to distract them from God’s path and religion. “Nay, you thought that We had not appointed to you a time” means that they thought no appointed return and reckoning awaited them, much like the denial in What! Did you then think that We had created you in vain and that you shall not be returned to Us? (23:115). Although worldly absorption explains their conduct, its deeper source is forgetfulness of resurrection, which is the root of forgetting God’s path and of evildoing: those who go astray from the path of God, they shall surely have a severe punishment because they forgot the day of reckoning (38:26).

Their conduct itself expresses belief that they will live permanently and not return to God. Alternatively, the statement may figuratively describe their disregard for God’s command and warning, as in . . . but you thought that God did not know most of what you did (41:22). It is also possible that it answers an unspoken excuse of ignorance; God knows best.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan explains that the book is placed before God for judgment. The guilty fear what it contains because it is the record of deeds, and their being called guilty shows that this rule extends to every guilty person, not only polytheists. The context most strongly indicates one book for reckoning all deeds, though this does not conflict with Qur’anic passages that speak of an individual book for each person, a book for each umma, and one comprehensive book. The alternative that “the book” merely means all books of deeds is not supported by the context.

Their cry, “Ah! woe to us!” expresses terror and astonishment at a record that omits neither a small nor a great act. “Small” and “great” stand for such things as sins, acts of disobedience, and trivial errors. The small is mentioned first because the terrifying point is that even what seems insignificant is recorded, as well as what is manifestly enormous. Wayl is a cry for perishing amid an affliction felt to be worse than death.

The commentary holds that, and what they had done they shall find present (there), begins a new point rather than merely explaining the completeness of the record. What they find present is their actual deeds, in forms appropriate to them, not simply the book. This embodiment of deeds clarifies why God does not deal unjustly with anyone: reward and punishment are attached to the deeds themselves, which return to and overtake their doers.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan presents the verse as a reminder of Iblīs’s rebellion: when God commanded the angels to bow before Adam, all obeyed except Iblīs, who was of the jinn and transgressed his Lord’s command. The event shows that Iblīs and his progeny are humanity’s enemies. They do not seek human good, and people must not follow their beautification of worldly pleasures and desires, turn away from God’s remembrance, or obey their invitation to falsehood.

The rhetorical question condemns taking Iblīs and his progeny as masters rather than God. Wilāya may mean obedience—treating them as objects of obedience instead of God, as exegetes have explained—but it may also, and more fittingly in light of the following verse, mean authority and regulation, or rubūbiyya. Just as idolaters worship angels in hope of benefit, they worship jinn to avert harm; thus they may take Iblīs and his offspring as gods and lords, worshiping and seeking their favor despite their enmity. The next verse’s denial that they witnessed creation specifically supports refuting their alleged regulating authority.

“Evil is (this) change for the unjust” condemns exchanging God for Iblīs. The reference to “the commandment of his Lord,” rather than “Our commandment,” serves this rhetorical purpose. Other questions concerning Iblīs’s inclusion in the command and his being of the jinn were addressed in the exegesis of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf [The Heights].
verses.51:
Al-Mizan takes the pronouns to refer to Iblīs and his progeny. Ishhād means making them witnesses, and ʿaḍud, literally the upper arm, here means a helper or one who lends a hand. The verse gives two proofs against the claim that they possess wilāyat al-tadbīr, authority to regulate the universe.

First, true direction of a thing requires comprehensive knowledge of it, its internal and external relations, origins, concomitants, and end. Iblīs and his progeny did not witness the creation of the heavens and earth or even their own creation; they are therefore ignorant of creation’s reality and of the conditions of their own being. Limited beings are veiled from what lies beyond them, including causes before their existence and consequences after it. They cannot consequently regulate themselves, let alone the cosmos, or be gods and lords besides God. This is a rational proof, provided one does not confuse human planning, conjecture, and inferred knowledge of unseen matters with God’s unerring cosmological direction and true eyewitness knowledge through which the unseen is seen.

Second, every species is instinctively directed toward its particular perfection, in accordance with the universal divine guidance expressed in He who gave to everything its creation, then guided it (to its goal) (20:50). Shayṭāns are mischief-makers whose characteristic is to lead astray. Their regulation of heavenly, earthly, or human affairs would contradict this divine sunna by making what leads astray an instrument of universal guidance; this is impossible. Thus God does not take those who lead others astray as helpers. The forms “I did not make them witnesses” and “nor would I” further show that God remains al-Qāhir and al-Muhaymin over them. Those who posit devils, angels, or others as partners in regulation generally claim not their independence, but a delegated possession from God; the verse denies this as well.

The commentary therefore retains the literal sense of ishhād and the contextual reference of both pronouns to Iblīs and his offspring. It rejects several alternatives. The view that witnessing is a metaphor for consultation lacks contextual evidence, and consultation does not itself establish authority. The further claim that consultation implies being created as one wishes, hence perfection and fitness to regulate, is excessively remote: it moves through several implications from witnessing to perfection. It also separates witnessing one’s own creation from witnessing the creation of heaven and earth, and improperly concedes that perfect contingent beings, such as favored angels, could be lords or autonomous regulators.

The view that the second pronoun means the satans witnessing one another’s creation misses the point, since no polytheist alleged that some satans regulate others. The view that the first pronoun denotes satans and the second unbelievers requires the two pronouns to have different referents.

Al-Rāzī’s reported view makes both pronouns refer to unbelievers who demanded that the Messenger expel poor believers, interpreting the verse as denying their partnership in regulating the world and thus rebuking their presumptuous demand. Al-Mizan calls this extremely unlikely: it breaks the immediate context, which is concerned with Satanic guardianship, and their demand had no connection with a claim to regulate worldly affairs. Related explanations that make them ignorant of what the Pen sempiternally wrote about happiness and misery, or deny that they possess a special standing such that their faith should be followed, are still more remote.

Finally, the interpretation that the pronouns denote angels and that only the final clause denies Satanic guardianship disrupts the logic. The preceding verse concerns the unbelievers’ alleged guardianship of satans, not angelic authority; introducing a refutation of angelic regulation is neither required by the verbal context nor by the passage’s purpose.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan calls this a third reminder: on the Day of Resurrection, the alleged link between polytheists and their associates will be exposed as false. God tells them to call the beings they considered His associates; when these do not answer, it becomes clear that God has no associates.

Mawbiq, derived from a word for perishing, may literally suggest a place of perishing between the two parties. The commentary rejects the interpretation that it must be hell, or a region of hell in which both worshipers and associates perish. “Associates” can include angels, prophets, and saints (awliyāʾ), perhaps chiefly so, and nothing confines the term here to rebellious jinn and humans.

Rather, making a mawbiq between them may mean abolishing their presumed relationship—the supposed proprietor-to-property and cause-to-effect connection—so that the relationship itself perishes without either party necessarily perishing. Their call is described as nidāʾ, a term used for calling one who is far away, indicating their distance from one another. This accords with: And We do not see with you your intercessors about whom you asserted that they were (God’s) associates in respect to you; certainly the ties between you are now cut off and what you asserted is gone from you (6:94), and Then We will say to those who associated others (with God): Keep where you are, you and your associates; then We shall separate them widely one from another and their associates would say: It was not us that you served (10:28).
verses.53: Al-Mizan explains that calling them “the guilty,” rather than only those who associated others with God, makes the threat applicable to all guilty people. Here ẓannu means certain knowledge, as shown by their having no place to turn away from the Fire. Muwāqiʿuhā means that they will fall into it; it may also suggest a twofold falling, in which they enter the Fire and the Fire falls upon them as it is fueled by them. Maṣrifan is a place to which one turns away, and they will find none: there is no escape.
verses.54: Al-Mizan explains jadal as disputatious and argumentative discourse. After the preceding reminders, verses 18:54–59 begin a warning of punishment: although the Qur’an sets forth every kind of example, human beings are especially prone to contention.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains that yuʾminū and yastaghfirū are joined: nothing prevents people from believing and seeking their Lord’s forgiveness once guidance reaches them, except their disposition to demand the fate of former peoples or punishment directly before their eyes. The former means desiring the divine destruction that overtook earlier nations. The latter means wanting to see punishment face to face; faith then, arising only after witnessing retribution, will not benefit them, as in But their belief was not going to profit them when they had seen Our punishment . . . (40:85).

Thus they do not seek the beneficial faith available to them. They seek either destruction without belief or, once punishment appears, desperate belief that brings no benefit. The verse’s language of their being prevented from belief is metaphorical: through evil intent they have turned their backs on the truth, rather than being compelled by an external prevention.
verses.56: Al-Mizan reads the verse as consoling the Prophet against grief over people’s rejection and their turning from God’s remembrance. Messengers are charged only with giving good news and warning, not with compelling a further response. The verse returns to the chapter’s earlier consolation, Then maybe you will kill yourself with grief over them, if they do not believe in this announcement, while also threatening the unbelievers who argue falsely to nullify the truth and mock God’s communications and warnings. Daḥḍ means perishing, idḥāḍ causing to perish or overcoming, and huzūʾ mockery.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan describes turning away after being reminded of God’s communications, while forgetting what one’s hands have sent ahead, as an especially immense wrong. Wrongdoing is proportionate to the one against whom it is committed; against God and His communications it is greater than any other. The reference to forgetting one’s prior deeds means that the Prophet should not be troubled by those who reject the truth and mock him, for he knows the communications are true.

The veils over their hearts and heaviness in their ears explain their turning away and their forgetting. Once God has placed these barriers, the verse expresses despair of their ever believing: they can neither comprehend the truth by themselves nor be guided by another’s call, since “in that case” emphatically denies that they will follow the right course.

Rūḥ al-maʿānī reports that the Jabriyya cite this verse for determinism, whereas the qadariyya cite the preceding verse for absolute free will, and al-ʿĀlūsī calls the juxtaposition a difficult test separating scholars firmly grounded in knowledge from mere followers. Al-Mizan holds both verses to be true: servants freely choose their acts, while God’s proprietary authority encompasses everything, including those acts. This is the doctrine of the People of the Household.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan explains that the wrongdoers’ corruption warrants punishment, indeed immediate punishment, since their continued life would produce further corruption. Yet punishment, though decreed, is not hastened: God postpones it to an appointed time known only to Him, from which they will have no refuge.

The opening attributes, “forgiving” and “the Lord of mercy,” explain this delay rather than cancel the certainty of retribution. Their deeds require punishment, but forgiveness removes its immediate consequence—its hastening—and mercy grants them life for the present. The verse is like a judgment preserving both claims: divine retribution establishes the inevitable punishment, while forgiveness and mercy defer it. “For them there is an appointed time” is a decree, not a merely descriptive statement.

Ghafūr is an intensive form, “Much-Forgiving.” Dhū l-Raḥma denotes the whole genus of mercy and is thus more comprehensive than raḥmān or raḥīm. Forgiveness first removes impediments; then Dhū l-Raḥma extends mercy wherever no impediment remains. This accounts for the combination of ghafūr with Dhū l-Raḥma.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that “towns” stands metonymically for their inhabitants, as shown by the pronouns and verb referring back to them, and that mahlik means an appointed time of destruction. Delaying destruction is therefore not new in the divine custom: God destroyed earlier peoples when they acted unjustly, but fixed a time for their destruction.

The threatened punishment is consequently worldly rather than punishment on the Day of Resurrection. If the threat addresses Quraysh’s elite, it may be the punishment at the Battle of Badr; if it addresses the Muslim community, it may be punishment at the end of time.
verses.60: Al-Mizan explains that lā abraḥ means that Moses would not cease travelling; its omitted predicate is supplied by “until I reach.” Majmaʿ al-baḥrayn is said to be the meeting-place of the Mediterranean and Persian Gulf, while the indefinite ḥuqub denotes a long time. Thus, God knows best, Moses tells his servant that he will continue until reaching the junction of the two seas, even if it takes a long time.
verses.61: Al-Mizan takes majmaʿa baynihima as a construction meaning the junction between the two waters. A common account holds that their provision was a salted or fried fish which revived there and entered the sea: the servant forgot to report the marvel, while Moses failed to check for the fish. But the commentary stresses that the verses do not expressly say the dead fish revived. Their literal sense may instead be that it was left on a rock, fell or was swept into the sea, and miraculously disappeared into its depths as though through a tunnel; some oral traditions likewise make its loss, rather than its revival, the sign. God knows best. Saraban likens the fish’s course through the water to a traveller vanishing into an impermeable tunnel.
verses.62: Al-Mizan notes that nasab, wasab, and tiʿb all denote weakness caused by exertion, while ghadaʾ is a daytime morning meal. Having passed the meeting-place of the two seas and become tired, Moses asked his servant to bring the fish they had carried as provisions.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan explains that the servant refers to their resting briefly at the rock at the junction of the two seas. He forgot not the fish itself, but the remarkable state he had witnessed and therefore failed to tell Moses of it; “nothing but the Shayṭān made me forget it—to speak of it” supports this reading. Even if the servant was Joshua b. Nūn, attributing such forgetfulness to the Shayṭān does not conflict with prophetic protection, which preserves prophets from what results in disobedience, not from every non-sinful annoyance; Job’s saying, “The Shayṭān has afflicted me with toil and torment” (38:41), provides an example.

The usual account is that the fish revived and entered the sea, though the alternative explanation of its simply falling in and sinking also applies here. “Wondrously” describes the extraordinary manner of its taking its way into the water, not an exclamation by Moses; the context rejects that alternative division of the speech.
verses.64: Al-Mizan explains that Moses recognized the affair of the fish as the sign they had been seeking, so the two returned by tracing their own footsteps. His words show that revelation had directed Moses to meet the learned servant at the junction of the two seas and had made the fish’s affair—whether its loss, revival, or entry into the sea—the marker of the place.
verses.65: Al-Mizan distinguishes ordinary mercies mediated by natural causes from esoteric mercies, such as prophethood and degrees of wilāya, in which those causes play no part. “Mercy from Us” likely denotes the latter because it is God’s gift alone; exegetes identify it as prophethood, supported by the plural divine voice, whereas singular language suits guardianship, though God knows best. Likewise, knowledge “from Ourselves” is gifted rather than acquired through sensation or thought, belongs exclusively to God’s friends, the awliyāʾ, and, as the story’s last verse indicates, interprets events.
verses.66: Al-Mizan explains rushd as correct understanding, the opposite of ghayy. Moses asks whether he may follow the learned servant so that he may teach him some of the knowledge taught to him, either knowledge by which Moses may be guided or simply that knowledge itself.
verses.67:
Al-Mizan takes the statement as an emphatic denial that Moses could show any patience at what al-Khiḍr would do while teaching him. Its force arises from inna, the indefinite ṣabr under negation, lan, and the denial of ability itself. Patience is impossible because it requires comprehensive khubr: knowledge of an event’s reality and interpretation, by which one knows that it must occur accordingly.

The point is not that Moses could not bear al-Khiḍr’s knowledge once explained, but that he could not endure seeing actions performed on the basis of that knowledge. Knowledge and direct sight evoke different responses: Moses was not agitated when God told him of the calf-worship, but was enraged when he later saw it. Thus al-Khiḍr foretells that Moses cannot withstand his method of instruction, not that he cannot receive the knowledge.
verses.68: Al-Mizan explains khubr as knowledge; grammatically, it is a specification (tamyīz).
verses.69: Al-Mizan explains that Moses made both his promise of patience and his promise not to disobey conditional on God’s will. He therefore neither lied when he proved impatient nor broke an unconditional promise when he asked questions despite al-Khiḍr’s instruction.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Khiḍr conditions Moses’ companionship on not questioning any troubling action he sees until al-Khiḍr himself initiates its explanation. The condition signals that Moses will witness matters difficult to endure and must wait patiently for their meaning.

The commentary finds remarkable mutual etiquette in their exchange. Though Moses was Kalīm Allāh, a Messenger Prophet, one endowed with constancy, and the recipient of the Torah, he asks rather than commands, calls accompanying al-Khiḍr “following,” presents teaching as al-Khiḍr’s favour, calls himself a learner, praises the knowledge as rushdan, asks only for some of what al-Khiḍr has been taught, and treats al-Khiḍr’s direction as an amr whose breach would be disobedience. His promise too is restrained and conditional: “If God pleases.”

Al-Khiḍr likewise does not bluntly reject him, but first indicates his likely impatience. After Moses’ promise, he does not command him to follow; he says, “If you would follow me.” Nor is the prohibition an independent, punishable nahy mawlawī: it is a condition of the voluntary following Moses requested.
verses.71: Al-Mizan explains that the two who proceeded were Moses and al-Khiḍr, not Moses’ servant. Moses’ charge that making a hole was done “to drown its passengers” treats an obvious, inevitable consequence as though it were intended, not as al-Khiḍr’s actual purpose. Imr denotes a great calamity.
verses.72: Al-Mizan explains this as al-Khiḍr’s reproach for Moses’ question and a reminder of his earlier warning that Moses would not be able to be patient with him.
verses.73: Al-Mizan takes Moses’ words as an apology: he asks not to be blamed for forgetting his promise and not to be burdened with difficulty in his affair. Although nisyān can mean failure to do something, actual forgetfulness is more likely; irhāq means constraining or imposing hardship.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan understands an omitted transition after the boat: they disembarked and went on. The verse is structured to emphasize Moses’ objection after the killing. Along with the following episode, it forms one continuous story of three successive objections by Moses, rather than three separate action-stories. Grammatically, making the hole is the result of the first conditional clause, whereas the killing, finding the wall, and restoring it belong within the later conditional clauses, whose results are Moses’ objections.

Zakiyya ordinarily suggests a boy innocent of sins because he has not reached adulthood, making Moses’ question a rhetorical condemnation. Yet ghulām can also mean an adult, and “who has not [slain] another person?” may mean one innocent of any capital offence. Nukr is an act regarded as abhorrent and unprecedented; killing is therefore presented as far worse than damaging the boat, an imr or grave calamity which may cause death but does not directly inflict it.
verses.75: Al-Mizan explains that the added “to you” sharpens al-Khiḍr’s reproach: Moses either did not heed the first warning or heard it without taking its personal force seriously—as though al-Khiḍr meant precisely Moses when he said, “you will not.”
verses.76: Al-Mizan explains that “after this” may refer either to this occasion or to this question: if Moses asks again, al-Khiḍr need no longer keep him as a companion. Qad balaghta min ladunnī means that al-Khiḍr will then have a sufficient excuse to separate, because his responsibility toward Moses will have ended.
verses.77: Al-Mizan explains that they asked the people, rather than the town itself, for food as guests; this wording also shows that al-Khiḍr repaired the wall in the townspeople’s presence. Their refusal was specifically a refusal of hospitality. The wall was metaphorically described as being on the point of collapse, and al-Khiḍr made it firm, though the verse does not state whether he did so miraculously or by ordinary construction. Moses’ suggestion of a wage implies the latter, since payment is ordinarily taken for non-miraculous work. As they were hungry, he meant that its recompense could have bought food.
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains that “this” may refer to Moses’ last remark, to the time of separation, or to the separation now due. Al-Khiḍr emphasizes “between me and you,” rather than merely “between us.” He separates only after the third objection: Moses had apologized after the first and requested another chance after the second, but then himself gave al-Khiḍr grounds to end their companionship if he questioned him again.
verses.79: Al-Mizan begins al-Khiḍr’s promised explanation by saying that he damaged the boat of poor men who earned their living at sea because a tyrannical king was seizing every sound boat by force. “Every boat” therefore means every undamaged boat. Warāʾ, literally “behind,” can also denote a threat of which one is unaware or from which one is distracted, whether spatially ahead or behind. The damage was meant to render the vessel undesirable and preserve it for its owners.
verses.80: Al-Mizan holds that, in view of the context and al-Khiḍr’s later statement that he did nothing of his own accord, fa-khashīnā most likely means metaphorically that “we were wary” out of kindness and compassion, not the literal emotional fear which God and His prophets do not experience. The boy would overburden his believing parents through impropriety and disbelief, either by leading them into disobedience and ingratitude through their intense love for him or, as the following phrase more strongly supports, because impropriety and unbelief are his own attributes.
verses.81: Al-Mizan explains “better than him in purity” as better in propriety (ṣalāḥ) and faith (īmān), the opposite of ṭughyān and kufr. Aqraba ruḥman means more caring toward his kin and relations, not merely more merciful; this supports reading the boy’s impropriety and unbelief as qualities that would burden his parents. Their faith was precious to God, so He commanded al-Khiḍr to kill the boy and replace him with a purer child more caring toward them.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan says it is possible that the “city” of the two orphans was not the town where the wall stood, since the wording directs attention to the boys and their guardians as absent from that town. The wall protected the orphans’ buried treasure from exposure and loss until they reached maturity. God’s mercy was the reason He willed this, and their deceased father’s righteousness was the reason for that mercy. The verse thus supports the view that a person’s righteousness may leave children a good and happy legacy.

The treasure does not imply that their father committed blameworthy hoarding. The verse does not say that he buried it; his being called righteous shows that it was not reprehensible even if he did. He may also have stored it for a good reason. Divine command can make outwardly grave acts permissible, as the story itself shows.

Al-Khiḍr’s statement that he did not act of his own accord means that all three acts were by God’s command. Taʾwīl, in Qur’anic usage, is the underlying reality, origin, benefit, purpose, or reason of a thing. The explanations al-Khiḍr gives are therefore the true reasons for the actions, not the apparent reasons Moses inferred: endangering passengers, unjustly killing a person, or acting imprudently in repairing a wall without provisions. Some say that al-Khiḍr’s speech also displays etiquette toward God: he attributes the apparently faulty damage to himself, uses “we” for what may be ascribed to himself and God, and attributes to God alone what belongs exclusively to divine lordship and governance.

Al-Mizan then recapitulates the Qur’anic story: God directed Moses to a servant possessing knowledge Moses lacked, at the junction of the two seas, marked by the fish’s revival or loss. Moses and his servant found the sign after the fish’s strange disappearance, returned, and met the servant. Moses sought to learn from him, accepted the condition not to question his actions, and nevertheless objected successively to the damaged boat, the slain boy, and the unrewarded repair of the wall. Al-Khiḍr then explained that he had preserved the poor sailors’ vessel from a king who seized sound boats, prevented the believing parents from being overburdened by their unbelieving, improper son and secured them a better replacement, and protected the righteous father’s orphans’ treasure until maturity. He then parted from Moses.

The commentary states that the Qur’an gives no account of al-Khiḍr beyond this story, the mercy and divinely taught knowledge granted him, and what is gleaned from prophetic traditions and traditions through the Imams of the People of the Household. A narration from Muḥammad b. ʿImāra on the authority of al-Ṣādiq calls him a Messenger Prophet sent to his people, whose sign was that dry wood or barren ground became green when he sat upon it; it names him Tālyā son of Mālik son of ʿĀbir son of Arfakhshad son of Sām son of Noah. A report cited in al-Durr al-manthūr from Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayra from the Prophet similarly explains the name al-Khiḍr by a white pelt turning green beneath him. By contrast, al-ʿAyyāshī’s narration from Burayd on one of the two Imams calls al-Khiḍr and Dhū l-Qarnayn learned men rather than prophets. The Qur’anic verses themselves do not plainly establish his prophethood, since ḥukm is said to come down to him.

Various narrations from the Imams indicate that al-Khiḍr remains alive; God’s granting a servant a miraculously long life is neither rationally impossible nor contradicted by decisive evidence. Some Sunnī reports explain this by claiming that he was from Adam’s loins and his death was deferred to reject the Antichrist (dajjāl), or that Adam prayed for his life until the Resurrection. Reports from both sects say that he drank from the Spring of Life in the darkness while serving in Dhū l-Qarnayn’s vanguard, receiving longevity when Dhū l-Qarnayn did not. These are aḥad reports and cannot be established by scripture, irrefutable Sunna, or reason. The commentary dismisses the many further marvellous tales about al-Khiḍr as unworthy of attention.
verses.83: Al-Mizan explains that the question concerns Dhū l-Qarnayn’s exploits, not his personal identity: the reply recounts his deeds, mentions only his nickname, and gives no real name. Dhikr may mean something worth mentioning about him, or some Qur’an concerning him; the latter is more likely. Minhu may mean either about Dhū l-Qarnayn or from God, and comprises the account that follows through the story’s end.
verses.84: Al-Mizan explains tamkīn as God’s enabling and facilitating Dhū l-Qarnayn’s sovereignty, giving him power to dispose of the land as he wished. A proposed derivation from makan would instead suggest stability immune to impediments, but rests on a mistaken view of the root letters. Granting him a sabab of everything means providing the means needed for great aims—such as intellect, knowledge, religion, strength, wealth, troops, extensive dominion, and ḥusn al-tadbīr. This divine blessing and the wisdom and strength evident in his career, deeds, and speech show the greatness of his affair.
verses.85: Al-Mizan explains that Dhū l-Qarnayn followed a course, taking a path toward the place where the sun sets.
verses.86:
Al-Mizan takes ḥattā to imply that Dhū l-Qarnayn travelled until he reached the western edge of civilization, where he found a people. His finding the sun setting in a black sea means that, from the shore and horizon beyond which no land was expected, it appeared to set in the sea. ʿAyn ḥamiʾa is said to mean a sea of black mud, applying to the Mediterranean; the alternative reading fiiʿaynin ḥāmiyya means a hot sea and may refer to Mediterranean regions near equatorial Africa, perhaps shores of Africa reached on his western journey.

God’s saying, “O Dhū l-Qarnayn,” does not establish that he was a prophet, since divine speech can be revelation to a prophet or inspiration to another. It nevertheless suggests that he may have been addressed through a prophet accompanying him, as Ṭālūt was guided by Israel’s prophet; this impression arises because God is referred to in the third person.

The words about chastising the people or doing them a benefit mean punishment or beneficial treatment. Although they may be read as permission to punish or forgive, or as suggesting the preference of doing good, Al-Mizan considers them most likely an inquiry into what he would do after conquering them: subjugate or forgive. This best fits his ensuing distinction between punishing wrongdoers and treating believing, righteous people well. The omitted object of “you punish” indicates that not all deserved punishment, whereas beneficence may be extended to an entire people containing both good and bad.
verses.87: Al-Mizan explains nukr and munkar as an unprecedented punishment, one the recipients had neither reckoned on nor expected. Some interpret ẓulm as polytheism and chastisement as killing, so that an unrepentant polytheist is killed. More likely, because the unjust are contrasted with those who believe and do good, ẓulm includes polytheists, outright unbelievers, and believers who do not associate others with God but fail to do good and spread mischief. Without that contrast, it would more naturally mean mischief-making, as just kings remove mischief-makers from their lands. Nothing confines the chastisement to killing.
verses.88: Al-Mizan explains that ṣāliḥan and al-ḥusnā are adjectives standing for implied nouns. Jazāʾan may mean that the believer’s good reward is a satisfactory fulfillment of obligation, that he has goodness specifically as reward, or, as an absolute object, that he will be greatly rewarded. Yusran means an easy word, and amrina most likely denotes a command concerning obligations: the believer will be given a duty that is easy rather than difficult.
verses.89: Al-Mizan explains that Dhū l-Qarnayn prepared the means for travel and journeyed to the eastern horizon, reaching an eastern desert where the sun rose over a nomadic people without shelter from it. Satr may mean protection through buildings and clothing, or buildings alone: they lived without houses and may have been naked. God’s attribution that He had given them no shelter alludes to their not yet having learned to build houses or tents, or to weave and sew clothing.

verses.91:
Al-Mizan takes kadhalika, “Even so,” as referring back to the condition just described, producing an emphatic comparison of a thing with itself; other proposed referents depart from the ordinary sense. “We had a full knowledge of what he had” refers to Dhū l-Qarnayn and is circumstantial: God knew all his provision, what he would do, and what would happen to him as he travelled and encountered that people.

Most likely, this alludes to his acting by God’s guidance and command, coming and going only as guided or ordered. The wording is thus akin in allusive force to statements that divine acts occur before God’s eyes, by His revelation, or within His encompassing knowledge. Other explanations—that it magnifies his affair, records the hardships of his journey as known to God, or magnifies his course—are less preferable.
verses.92: Al-Mizan explains sadd as a mountain or any obstruction that blocks a way; al-saddayn therefore means two mountains. Dhū l-Qarnayn found a people near them who could hardly understand speech. This may indicate their simplicity and superficial understanding, though it may also allude to the strangeness of their language and its remoteness from languages known to others.
verses.93: Al-Mizan explains sadd as a mountain or any obstruction that blocks a way; al-saddayn therefore means two mountains. verses.94: Al-Mizan considers the speakers to be the people found between the two mountains. Gog and Magog were likely two generations of people who came from behind the mountains to raid them, killing, wounding, and plundering; the rational plural pronoun and the barrier’s location support this. Kharaj is money taken from one’s property for needed expenditure. They therefore offered Dhū l-Qarnayn payment to build a barrier preventing Gog and Magog from crossing and attacking them.
verses.95: Al-Mizan explains that Dhū l-Qarnayn rejected the offered kharaj because the abundance and strength with which his Lord had established him were better than their money. Their offer was thus wages for constructing the barrier. He instead asked for quwwa—whatever enabled the work, including workers and materials—and promised a radm, a barrier or, more specifically, a strong fortified barrier. On the latter meaning, he promised not merely the sadd they requested but something stronger than they expected, using such means as iron blocks, molten brass, and bellows.
verses.96: Al-Mizan explains zubar as blocks, al-ṣadafayn as the two sides of the mountains, and qiṭr as copper or molten brass. The people supplied the blocks of iron—part of the quwwa Dhū l-Qarnayn had requested and the principal material of a strong barrier—and he erected the barrier between the mountain sides. The command to blow implies placing bellows against it to heat the iron. When it became fire, or like fire in appearance or heat, he ordered molten brass to be poured over it, sealing its cracks and gaps so that nothing could penetrate it.
verses.97: Al-Mizan explains that the two forms isṭāʿū and istaṭāʿū both mean “they were able,” here negated. The pronouns refer to Gog and Magog: they could neither scale the barrier, because of its height, nor make a naqb—a hole, especially one in a wall or skin—because of its strength.
verses.98:
Al-Mizan explains that after building the barrier, Dhū l-Qarnayn called it a mercy from his Lord: protection by which the evil of Gog and Magog was restrained from nations. Dakkāʾ denotes being beaten flat and thus the barrier’s destruction; alternatively it evokes a camel without a hump and is metaphorical.

The mercy will endure until God’s promise comes, when He will level the barrier with the ground. The promise may be one specifically concerning the barrier’s flattening near the Hour, making this an apocalyptic prediction reported by Dhū l-Qarnayn, or it may be God’s general promise of the Hour, when mountains and the world are destroyed. His final assertion emphasizes that his Lord’s promise is true.
verses.99:
Al-Mizan takes the plural pronouns to refer to people. On that day they will be driven about by terror like the swelling sea, pressed against one another as order gives way to chaos; divine mercy and care will not set their affair right. The verse fills out the earlier statement that God will level the barrier when His promise comes and predicts a future apocalyptic event, comparable to the release of Gog and Magog.

Tark, “We will leave,” retains its ordinary sense, the opposite of taking, rather than meaning making. These are God’s words, not the continuation of Dhū l-Qarnayn’s speech, as the shift from third person to the first-person plural of majesty shows. The trumpet is the second blast, the one that resurrects, as indicated by the subsequent universal gathering and exposure of hell to the unbelievers.

verses.101: Al-Mizan explains that these are the unbelievers: God placed a barrier between them and His remembrance, covering their eyes and removing their capacity to hear. Thus the route to truth has been cut off. Truth is attained either by seeing God’s words and being guided by what they indicate, or by hearing wisdom, warnings, narratives, and lessons; these people possess neither sight nor hearing in that sense.
verses.102:
Al-Mizan treats the question as rhetorical. Majmaʿ al-bayān explains it as asking whether deniers of God’s oneness think that taking lords besides Him will help them and ward off His punishment; hell prepared for the unbelievers supports this sense. A second explanation, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, is that they think they may take gods besides Him without incurring His anger or punishment. A third makes their taking servants as guardians the first object of ḥasiba, with the unstated second object being whether this will avail them and prevent punishment. A fourth denies that their ittikhādh is real ittikhādh at all, since true taking must be mutual and those taken disown them: They shall say: Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not they . . . (34:41).

The explanations rank in that order, and the first is best. The chapter’s context concerns people seduced by worldly adornment, relying on apparent causes and guardians besides God in the belief that these will suffice them and ward off harm. What confronts them after the trumpet and gathering refutes that belief. This reading also permits an and its relative phrase to serve as both objects of ḥasiba, as elsewhere, despite some grammatical objections. It is further supported by the following verses and by the recitation attributed to ʿAlī and others, a fa ḥasbu: “What! Is taking My servants as guardians instead of Me enough for them?”

“My servants” can refer to angels, jinn, and perfect humans worshiped by idolaters. Some exegetes restrict it to the Messiah, angels, and similar favored beings, excluding shayṭāns because ʿibādi is supposedly honorific. Al-Mizan rejects this: the context does not call for honoring, and min dūni shows that the unbelievers are idolaters who acknowledge God’s divinity but worship intercessory associates instead of Him. It does not describe the People of the Book, who affirm God’s guardianship while also taking the Messiah as guardian. Thus “My servants” excludes the Messiah and humans like him and is confined to the idolaters’ gods; “those who disbelieve” means idolaters alone.

Hell as their “entertainment” is a scornful analogy: the hereafter is like a guest’s dwelling and hell like the entertainment offered on arrival. The later statement that they receive no weight on the Day of Resurrection sharpens the image, as though they enter hell immediately, in requital for their scorn of God’s signs and messengers.
verses.103:
Al-Mizan takes the second-person address to be an allusion to the polytheists, who are identified more explicitly as those who disbelieve in their Lord’s signs and His meeting. Denial of prophethood and resurrection is, in this sense, the mark of the polytheists meant by “the greatest losers in (their) deeds.” The expression bi-l-akhsarīn ʿamalan is not intended to enumerate varieties of deeds or to state that loss encompasses every deed.

The next verse explains their condition: ḍalāl al-saʿy, “straying of labor,” is the loss of an undertaking that fails to attain its intended profit, as though the labor has lost its way and reached the opposite of its aim. Ordinary loss through inexperience, ignorance of the proper course, or circumstance may still be remedied: one may recognize it, begin again, and recover what was missed. The gravest loss is instead to suffer harm while believing oneself to be profiting, unable to perceive otherwise; such loss has no hope of removal.

Human striving in worldly life aims at happiness. One who follows truth reaches true happiness, while one who errs without recognizing the error may yet be saved. But one who adopts falsehood as truth becomes veiled from every hint of truth: the soul beautifies for him the arrogance and ignorant zeal in which he is immersed. His labor is therefore the greatest loss, because it cannot be expected to turn into happiness. Their conviction that their work is good, despite truth and the futility of their deeds being made manifest, arises from attraction to worldly adornments and vanities and immersion in desire. This prevents them from following truth or heeding those who call to it and to innate belief, as in: And they denied them unjustly and proudly while their soul had been convinced of them . . . (27:14), And when it is said to him, guard against (the punishment of) God; pride carries him off to sin . . . (2:206). Persisting in desire, stubbornness, and pride is thus their satisfaction with their own way and their belief that it is good.
verses.104:
Al-Mizan presents this as a second explanation of “the greatest losers in (their) deeds.” Since “signs” is unrestricted, it includes signs on the horizons and in souls, as well as the miracles brought by prophets and messengers; the Prophet himself is among the signs. Disbelief in them is disbelief in prophethood. “His meeting” means return to God, namely the spirit’s return to the body. Thus the description essentially concerns denial of prophethood and resurrection, which the commentary considers exclusive to idolaters.

Their deeds are forfeited because they do not act for God’s sake, seek neither reward nor happiness in the hereafter, and are not motivated by remembrance of the Day of Reckoning. Since weight on the Day of Resurrection consists in the measure of good deeds—And the measuring out on that day will be just; then as for him whose measure (of good deeds) is heavy, those are they who shall be successful; And as for him whose measure (of good deeds) is light, those are they who have made their souls suffer loss . . . (7:8–9)—their forfeited deeds leave them with no good deeds and hence no weight.

verses.106: Al-Mizan explains that dhalika refers emphatically to the matter of their being as previously described. “Their recompense is hell” newly states the consequence of their condition: they disbelieved and further compounded that disbelief by mocking God’s signs and messengers.
verses.107: Al-Mizan notes differing reported derivations for firdaws, including senses connected with a garden or vine garden; it is also said in Arabic to mean a tree-enclosed garden in which vines predominate. Some exegetes infer from firdaws being prepared as entertainment for believers who do good deeds, and hell for unbelievers, that indescribable reward and punishment exist beyond heaven and hell. This view may be supported by: So no soul knows what is hidden for them of that which will refresh the eyes . . . (32:17) and . . . and what they never thought of shall become plain to them from God (39:47).
verses.108: Al-Mizan explains that baghy means “seeking” and ḥiwal literally means “a change”; thus those abiding in firdaws will not seek removal from it.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan explains that kalima may be singular or plural and is often used in the Qur’an for what God has said and ruled. God does not speak by opening a mouth: His “word” is His action and the existence He effuses, as in His saying to a thing, “Be, and it is” (16:40). It is called a word because it signifies Him; hence the Messiah is called God’s word. In this broad sense, every existing thing (ʿayn) is a word from Him, since it indicates Him.

The Qur’an, however, applies “word” specifically to what indicates God plainly, without concealment, impediment, or changeability, such as the Messiah and definitive judgments. Therefore, “the words of my Lord” in this verse cannot mean the things God knows, His decrees, His promises of reward and punishment, or the other interpretations reported from exegetes.

The verse means that, if the sea were used as ink to inscribe the words in accordance with the realities to which they refer, it would be exhausted before God’s words. If another sea were added, it too would run dry. An exegete interprets mithlihi as the genus of like seas rather than one single additional sea, and explains the point by the inability of the finite to record God’s infinite knowledge. Al-Mizan accepts the conclusion that the words are infinite, but holds that the reason is not simply finitude and infinity: the realities denoted by the words, and the words in relation to them, exceed measure. Were the hypothetical realized, even each atom of the sea could not record its own indication of God’s beauty and sublimity, much less anything else.

The repetition of “sea” and “my Lord,” rather than using pronouns, serves confirmation and emphasis. Calling Him “Lord” and annexing it to the first-person pronoun also honors the one to whom it is annexed.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan explains that “I am only a mortal like you” restricts the Prophet to a humanity identical with that of other people. It denies that his claim to prophethood entails divinity or power over the unseen—the basis on which they demanded from him what only God knows and can do—while affirming only that revelation comes to him by God’s command.

“Your god is one God” establishes monotheism: the God of all people is one. The ensuing command summarizes the religious call: one must do good solely for God and associate no one with Him in one’s service. Hope of meeting the Lord means returning to Him for reckoning and requital; without this, there would be no reason to embrace religion and faith. Even hope, rather than certainty, of resurrection is enough to require caution against possible harm. “Meeting” may also mean attaining an esteem that is hoped for rather than certain.

Good deeds necessarily follow from refraining from association in worship, for affirming God’s oneness while associating others with Him in one’s acts is contradictory. If God is one, He alone is the object of worship, without any other being joined to Him. Return to and judgment by God also follow from His full divinity: possessing every perfection, doing right, and ruling justly, He cannot create in vain or treat believers who do good as He treats evildoers, as indicated in (38:27–28). The verse thus also bears on those who believe in God while associating others with Him (12:106).
